phy_ocrb.0.0.summary: Light is just one member of a whole family of waves called the **electromagnetic (EM) spectrum**: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. They are all transverse waves that transfer energy, and they all travel at the **same speed in a vacuum (space): 300 000 km/s, or 3 x 10^8 m/s**. What makes them different is their wavelength and frequency: going from radio to gamma, wavelength gets shorter, frequency gets higher and each photon carries more energy.

core.p: OCR expects you to recall that **light is one part of a continuous spectrum of electromagnetic radiation**. All EM radiation is the same kind of thing: an oscillating electric and magnetic disturbance that travels outwards from its source carrying energy.
bullets: EM waves are **transverse**: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
EM waves **transfer energy from a source to an absorber** without transferring matter.
EM waves **do not need a medium**: they can travel through a vacuum, which is why sunlight and starlight reach us across space.
The spectrum is **continuous**: there are no gaps, and the boundaries between regions are not sharp (the regions overlap).
Our eyes can detect only a very narrow band of the spectrum, which we call visible light.

callouts.p: A continuous family of transverse waves, from radio waves to gamma rays, which all travel at the same speed in a vacuum but have different wavelengths and frequencies.

core.p: You must be able to put the seven regions in order. Learn the order from **longest wavelength (lowest frequency)** to **shortest wavelength (highest frequency)**.
bullets: **Radio waves** - longest wavelength (metres to kilometres), lowest frequency.
**Microwaves** - wavelength roughly millimetres to centimetres.
**Infrared (IR)** - just longer than red light.
**Visible light** - red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
**Ultraviolet (UV)** - just shorter than violet light.
**X-rays** - very short wavelength.
**Gamma rays** - shortest wavelength, highest frequency.
Memory aid: **R**abbits **M**eet **I**n **V**ery **U**nusual e**X**pensive **G**ardens.

callouts.p: Exam questions often give a partly filled spectrum and ask you to fill in the gaps. Check which end the question starts from - some start with gamma, some with radio.

core.h: Wavelength and frequency change in opposite directions
core.p: Every EM wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum. Because wave speed = frequency x wavelength, if the speed is fixed then **a shorter wavelength must mean a higher frequency**. Frequency and wavelength are **inversely proportional** for EM waves.
bullets: **Wavelength** is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (for example crest to crest), measured in metres.
**Frequency** is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
1 Hz = 1 wave per second; 1 kHz = 1000 Hz; 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz; 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.
Halve the wavelength and the frequency doubles (speed stays 3 x 10^8 m/s).
So going from radio to gamma: wavelength goes **down**, frequency goes **up**.

callouts.p: For EM waves in a vacuum: higher frequency = shorter wavelength, because v = f x lambda and v is the same for all of them.

core.p: EM radiation transfers energy in tiny packets called **photons**. The energy of each photon depends on the frequency of the radiation: **the higher the frequency, the more energy each photon carries**. This is why gamma rays and X-rays can do so much more damage than radio waves.
bullets: A **photon** is a packet (quantum) of electromagnetic energy.
Photon energy is **proportional to frequency**: double the frequency, double the energy of each photon.
Radio photons carry very little energy each; gamma photons carry the most.
The **energy of one photon** is different from the **total energy** delivered: that also depends on how many photons arrive (the intensity).
High-energy photons (high-frequency UV, X-rays, gamma) carry enough energy to **ionise** atoms - this links to the hazards of these regions.

callouts.p: A packet of energy carried by electromagnetic radiation; its energy is proportional to the frequency of the radiation.
A bright red lamp sends more total energy than a dim UV lamp, but each UV photon still carries more energy than each red photon. Do not confuse photon energy with brightness.

core.p: The **intensity** of radiation is the energy arriving per second on each square metre of surface. It depends on how many photons arrive and how much energy each one carries.
bullets: Intensity = energy arriving per second per unit area.
Intensity **decreases with distance** from a source because the energy spreads out over a bigger area.
Intensity is also reduced if some radiation is absorbed by the material it passes through.
The **total energy** absorbed by an object depends on the intensity and on how long it is exposed.

callouts.p: The energy arriving at a surface each second, per unit area.

core.h: The speed of EM radiation in space
core.p: All electromagnetic waves travel at **exactly the same speed through a vacuum: 300 000 km/s (3 x 10^8 m/s)**. This is often just called the speed of light, but it is the speed of every EM wave, from radio to gamma.
bullets: Speed of EM radiation in a vacuum = **300 000 000 m/s = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s = 300 000 km/s**.
It is the fastest speed anything can travel.
In air the speed is almost exactly the same, so you can use 3 x 10^8 m/s for air too.
In denser materials like glass or water EM waves slow down - this causes refraction (covered in P1.3).
Light from the Sun takes about **8 minutes** to reach the Earth; light from the Moon about 1.3 s.
Because the speed is so huge, light from a lightning flash reaches you almost instantly, while the sound (about 340 m/s) arrives later.

callouts.p: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum: 3 x 10^8 m/s. They differ in wavelength and frequency, NOT in speed.

core.p: You can use wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda) for any EM wave, using v = 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum or air.
bullets: v = f x lambda, so f = v / lambda and lambda = v / f.
v in m/s, f in Hz, lambda in m - always convert units first.
nm = nanometre = 10^-9 m; micrometre = 10^-6 m; mm = 10^-3 m.
kHz = 10^3 Hz, MHz = 10^6 Hz, GHz = 10^9 Hz.
Use standard form on your calculator and give answers to sensible significant figures.

callouts.p: Most lost marks in EM calculations come from forgetting to change MHz to Hz or nm to m before substituting.

core.h: Distance, speed and time in space
core.p: Because EM radiation travels at a known speed, you can work out how long a signal takes to travel, or how far away something is, using **distance = speed x time**.
bullets: distance (m) = speed (m/s) x time (s).
time = distance / speed.
Radio signals to and from spacecraft or satellites take a measurable time; for a signal there and back, double the distance.
Astronomers use the light-year: the distance light travels in one year.

callouts.p: If a signal is reflected (for example radar off the Moon), the time measured is for the round trip, so halve it to find the one-way distance.

core.p: Visible light is the narrow band our eyes detect. Different wavelengths of visible light are seen as **different colours**.
bullets: Red has the **longest wavelength** (about 700 nm) and lowest frequency of visible light.
Violet has the **shortest wavelength** (about 400 nm) and highest frequency of visible light.
White light is a mixture of all the colours.
Just beyond red (longer wavelength) is infrared; just beyond violet (shorter wavelength) is ultraviolet - this is where the names come from.

callouts.p: Infra means below (lower frequency than red); ultra means beyond (higher frequency than violet).

core.h: What all EM waves share and how they differ
core.p: Exam questions often ask what is the same and what is different about two kinds of EM radiation. Use the word bank below.
bullets: Same: all are **transverse** waves.
Same: all travel at **3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum**.
Same: all **transfer energy** and can travel through a vacuum.
Same: all can be reflected, refracted, absorbed and transmitted.
Different: **wavelength**, **frequency** and **energy of each photon**.
Different: how they interact with materials (for example X-rays pass through flesh but light does not).

core.p: The grade 9 idea is to chain the reasoning together: shorter wavelength means higher frequency, higher frequency means higher-energy photons, and high-energy photons can ionise atoms and damage living cells.
bullets: Chain: short wavelength -> high frequency -> high photon energy -> can ionise -> can damage DNA.
Low-frequency radiation (radio, microwave, infrared) is **non-ionising**: its photons do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms; it mainly causes heating if absorbed.
High-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma rays are **ionising**.
Whether a dose is harmful also depends on intensity and exposure time.

callouts.p: Higher-frequency ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have photons with enough energy to ionise.

analogy.p: Think of the EM spectrum as a giant piano keyboard stretching for kilometres. Every key makes the same kind of sound wave, and every note travels to your ear at the same speed, but the keys at one end give long, low notes (radio waves) and the keys at the other end give short, high notes (gamma rays). Our eyes can only hear one octave in the middle (visible light). Where it breaks down: sound is a longitudinal wave that needs air and travels at about 340 m/s, while EM waves are transverse, travel through a vacuum at 3 x 10^8 m/s, and come in photons whose energy grows with frequency - a higher piano note is not more dangerous.

terms.d: The continuous range of electromagnetic waves, from radio waves to gamma rays, ordered by wavelength or frequency.
A transverse wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that transfers energy and can travel through a vacuum.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
The distance between a point on one wave and the same point on the next wave, measured in metres.
The number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one wave per second.
The distance travelled by a wave per second; v = f x lambda.
The speed of all EM waves in a vacuum: 3 x 10^8 m/s (300 000 km/s).
A space with no particles of matter in it, such as outer space.
A packet of energy carried by EM radiation; its energy is proportional to frequency.
The energy arriving per second per unit area of a surface.
The narrow band of the EM spectrum that human eyes can detect, about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).
EM radiation with wavelengths just longer than red light.
EM radiation with wavelengths just shorter than violet light.
Radiation whose photons have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms or molecules (higher-frequency UV, X-rays, gamma).
One billionth of a metre, 10^-9 m.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy.
mistakes.r: All EM waves travel at the same speed (3 x 10^8 m/s) in a vacuum; gamma rays have a higher frequency and shorter wavelength, not a higher speed.

mistakes.w: Higher frequency means longer wavelength.
mistakes.r: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, because speed is constant and v = f x lambda.

mistakes.w: EM waves are longitudinal / need a medium like sound.
mistakes.r: EM waves are transverse and can travel through a vacuum.

mistakes.w: Putting microwaves after infrared, or X-rays after gamma.
mistakes.r: Order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

mistakes.w: The speed of light is 3 x 10^8 km/s.
mistakes.r: It is 3 x 10^8 m/s, which is 300 000 km/s.

mistakes.w: Using 100 MHz as 100 in v = f x lambda.
mistakes.r: Convert to hertz first: 100 MHz = 1.0 x 10^8 Hz.

mistakes.w: Radio waves are a type of sound wave.
mistakes.r: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves; a radio converts the signal they carry into sound.

mistakes.w: Bright light carries more energy per photon than dim light.
mistakes.r: Photon energy depends on frequency only; brightness (intensity) depends on how many photons arrive.

exam.q: Which of these travels fastest in a vacuum: radio waves, visible light, X-rays, or do they all travel at the same speed?
model: They all travel at the same speed (3 x 10^8 m/s).
exam.tip: Same speed in a vacuum is the most tested EM fact.

exam.q: State the speed of electromagnetic radiation in space. Give the unit.
exam.tip: Always include the unit; check km/s versus m/s.

exam.q: Put these in order of increasing frequency: X-rays, microwaves, visible light, gamma rays, radio waves.
model: Radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays, gamma rays.
One mark if one adjacent pair is swapped.
exam.tip: Increasing frequency means starting from the radio end.

exam.q: Infrared and ultraviolet are both parts of the EM spectrum. Give one property they have in common and one way in which they differ.
model: Common: both transverse / both travel at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum / both can travel through a vacuum / both transfer energy.
Differ: ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength / higher frequency / higher photon energy.
exam.tip: Use comparative words: shorter, higher.

exam.q: Explain why X-ray photons carry more energy than infrared photons.
model: X-rays have a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) than infrared.
Photon energy is proportional to (increases with) frequency.
exam.tip: Link energy to frequency, not to speed.

exam.q: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. Speed of EM waves = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
model: Convert: 100 MHz = 1.0 x 10^8 Hz.
lambda = 3.0 m.
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then substitute, and show the unit conversion.

exam.q: Green light has a wavelength of 5.0 x 10^-7 m. Calculate its frequency.
model: f = v / lambda.
exam.tip: Enter standard form carefully using the x10 or EXP key.

exam.q: The Sun is 1.5 x 10^11 m from the Earth. Calculate how long light takes to travel from the Sun to the Earth, in minutes.
model: time = distance / speed = 1.5 x 10^11 / 3.0 x 10^8.
= 8.3 minutes (approximately 8 minutes).
exam.tip: Watch for the unit the question asks for - convert seconds to minutes.

exam.q: Explain why we can see the Sun but cannot hear it, even though the Sun is very noisy.
model: Light is an EM wave which can travel through a vacuum (space).
Sound needs a medium (particles) to travel through, and space is a vacuum.
exam.tip: Contrast EM waves with sound by the need for a medium.

exam.q: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum. Your answer should include the order of the regions and how wavelength, frequency, photon energy and speed change across it.
model: Family of transverse waves that transfer energy and travel through a vacuum.
Order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
Wavelength decreases from radio to gamma.
Frequency increases from radio to gamma.
Photon energy increases with frequency, so gamma photons have most energy.
All travel at the same speed, 3 x 10^8 m/s, in a vacuum; so f and lambda are inversely related (v = f x lambda).
exam.tip: For 6 markers, cover every idea in a logical order: what it is, the order, the trends, and why they link.

worked.q: A mobile phone signal uses microwaves of frequency 1.8 GHz. Calculate the wavelength.
steps: Write the equation: v = f x lambda, so lambda = v / f.
Convert: 1.8 GHz = 1.8 x 10^9 Hz.
Substitute: lambda = 3.0 x 10^8 / 1.8 x 10^9.
Calculate: lambda = 0.1667 m.
worked.ans: lambda = 0.17 m (about 17 cm).

worked.q: A radar pulse is sent from Earth to the Moon and its reflection is detected 2.56 s later. Calculate the distance to the Moon.
steps: The pulse travels there and back, so one-way time = 2.56 / 2 = 1.28 s.
distance = speed x time.
distance = 3.0 x 10^8 x 1.28.
distance = 3.84 x 10^8 m.

worked.q: Red light has wavelength 700 nm and violet light 400 nm. Which has the higher frequency, and by what factor?
steps: Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength because speed is constant.
Violet has the shorter wavelength, so the higher frequency.
worked.ans: Violet light, with a frequency 1.75 times that of red light (so its photons carry 1.75 times as much energy).

phy_ocrb.0.1.summary: When EM radiation meets a material it can be **reflected**, **transmitted** or **absorbed** (and when transmitted it may be refracted), and what happens depends on both the material and the **wavelength** of the radiation. Radiation is emitted and absorbed by changes in **electrons, nuclei and molecules**: the higher the energy change, the higher the frequency of the radiation involved. Absorbed radiation transfers energy that usually causes **heating**, but photons of high-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to cause **ionisation**.

core.h: Three things that can happen at a material
core.p: When electromagnetic radiation hits an object, the energy it carries can go three ways. Often more than one happens at once, and the fractions add up to all of the incoming radiation.
bullets: **Reflected**: the radiation bounces back off the surface (a mirror reflects light; metal reflects radio waves and microwaves).
**Transmitted**: the radiation passes through the material and carries on (glass transmits visible light; flesh transmits X-rays).
**Absorbed**: the radiation is taken in by the material and its energy is transferred to the material, usually making it hotter.
Radiation that is transmitted may also be **refracted** (change direction) when it crosses the boundary at an angle.
reflected + transmitted + absorbed = all of the incident radiation.

callouts.p: When radiation is taken in by a material and its energy is transferred to the material.
When radiation passes through a material.

core.p: OCR wants you to recall that **different substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect EM radiation in ways that vary with wavelength**. The same material can behave completely differently for two regions of the spectrum.
bullets: **Glass** transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet and long-wave infrared.
**Soft tissue** (skin, muscle) transmits most X-rays, but **bone absorbs** them, which is why X-ray images work.
**Water** strongly absorbs microwaves of the frequency used in microwave ovens.
**Metals** reflect radio waves, microwaves and light; they are used for dishes and microwave oven walls.
The **atmosphere** transmits visible light and radio waves but absorbs most UV (in the ozone layer), X-rays and gamma rays.
Carbon dioxide and water vapour transmit visible light but **absorb infrared**.

callouts.p: Whether radiation is absorbed, transmitted or reflected depends on the material AND on the wavelength (frequency) of the radiation.

core.p: When radiation is absorbed, energy is transferred to the material. For most radiation this simply makes the particles move or vibrate more, so the **temperature rises**.
bullets: Infrared and microwaves absorbed by skin or food cause **heating**.
The amount of heating depends on the **intensity** of the radiation and the **time** of exposure.
Absorbed radiation does not just disappear - the energy is transferred to the absorber.
Radio waves absorbed by an aerial cause an alternating current in it (useful for receivers).

callouts.p: Never say the radiation is destroyed. Say its energy is transferred to the material, which usually heats it.

core.h: How radiation is emitted and absorbed by atoms
core.p: Electrons in an atom can only have certain energies, called **energy levels**. Radiation is emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps between levels. Changes in atoms and nuclei can generate radiation over a **wide frequency range**, or be caused by absorbing a range of radiations.
bullets: **Absorption**: an electron absorbs a photon and moves to a higher energy level (further from the nucleus).
**Emission**: an electron drops to a lower energy level and emits a photon.
The energy of the photon equals the energy difference between the levels.
Bigger energy jump -> higher-energy photon -> higher frequency radiation.
Electrons in the outer parts of atoms produce and absorb **visible light and ultraviolet** (for example in hot gases, neon lamps, the Sun).
This is why hot gases give out light of particular colours.

callouts.p: Photon energy = energy difference between the two electron energy levels. A bigger gap gives a higher-frequency photon.

core.h: Which part of matter produces which radiation
core.p: Different regions of the spectrum come from different kinds of change in matter. The bigger the energy change, the higher the frequency of the radiation.
bullets: **Gamma rays** are emitted by changes in the **nucleus** of unstable (radioactive) atoms - the biggest energy changes.
**X-rays** are produced when **electrons** change energy close to the nucleus (inner electrons), or when fast electrons are suddenly stopped by a metal target in an X-ray tube.
**Ultraviolet and visible light** come from **electrons** in atoms changing energy level, for example in very hot objects and in fluorescent lamps.
**Infrared** is emitted and absorbed by **molecules vibrating**; all warm objects emit infrared.
**Microwaves** are absorbed by molecules such as water, making them rotate and vibrate more, which heats them.
**Radio waves** are produced by **oscillating electrons (alternating currents) in electrical circuits and aerials**.

core.p: If a photon carries enough energy, it can knock an electron completely out of an atom or molecule. The atom is left with an overall positive charge - it has become an **ion**. This process is called **ionisation**.
bullets: Ionisation = **removing an electron from an atom or molecule**, forming a positive ion.
Only **high-frequency** radiation has photons with enough energy: higher-frequency **ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays**.
These are called **ionising radiation**.
Radio, microwave, infrared and visible light are **non-ionising**: each photon has too little energy, no matter how intense the beam.
Ions are very reactive, so ionisation in living cells can trigger chemical reactions that damage molecules such as **DNA**.
Ionisation happens photon by photon: it depends on the energy of each photon (frequency), not just total energy.

callouts.p: The process in which an atom or molecule gains or loses an electron to become a charged ion; ionising radiation removes electrons.

callouts.t: Intensity does not make it ionising
callouts.p: A very bright beam of visible light still cannot ionise, because each photon has too little energy. It may heat strongly instead.

fig.cap: Ionisation: a high-energy photon (for example a gamma ray) gives an electron enough energy to escape, leaving the atom as a positive ion.

core.p: Absorbed radiation always transfers energy, but the effect depends on photon energy. A grade 9 answer separates the two effects clearly.
bullets: **Low-frequency** radiation (radio, microwave, infrared): absorbed energy causes **heating** only.
**Visible light**: mostly heating, and can trigger some chemical changes (for example in the retina or in photosynthesis).
**High-frequency** radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma): as well as heating, can cause **ionisation** and damage cells.
Danger from heating depends on intensity and time; danger from ionisation depends on photon energy, dose and time.

callouts.p: In 'explain why X-rays are more dangerous than microwaves' answers, mention: higher frequency, higher energy photons, can ionise, damage DNA/cells. Microwaves only cause heating.

core.p: The Earth's atmosphere is a big real-life example of wavelength-dependent absorption and transmission.
bullets: Visible light and most radio waves are **transmitted** through the atmosphere, which is why we can see the Sun and use radio telescopes on the ground.
Most UV is **absorbed by the ozone layer** in the upper atmosphere, protecting living things.
X-rays and gamma rays from space are **absorbed** high in the atmosphere, so X-ray telescopes must be on satellites.
Some infrared is absorbed by **greenhouse gases** (carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane).

core.p: Reflection sends radiation back from a surface. Smooth shiny surfaces reflect well; matt dark surfaces absorb more.
bullets: Metal surfaces reflect radio waves and microwaves - used in satellite dishes and the metal walls and door mesh of microwave ovens.
Mirrors and white surfaces reflect visible light well.
Shiny surfaces reflect infrared well; matt black surfaces absorb infrared well.
Radar works by microwaves or radio waves reflecting from aircraft and ships.

core.h: Transmission and the intensity of radiation
core.p: Even a material that mostly transmits will absorb a little. The further radiation travels through an absorber, the more is absorbed, so the **intensity falls**.
bullets: Thicker or denser absorbers absorb more radiation.
Lead absorbs X-rays and gamma rays strongly - used for shielding.
Thick concrete absorbs gamma rays.
On an X-ray image, areas where X-rays are absorbed (bone) look white because fewer X-rays reach the detector.

callouts.p: Score marks by naming exactly what happens: 'the X-rays are transmitted by soft tissue but absorbed by bone'.

core.p: Every interaction can be explained by the energy of the photon matching what the material's particles can do with it.
bullets: If a material's particles can take in the photon's energy (an electron jump, a molecular vibration, a rotation), the radiation is likely **absorbed**.
If nothing in the material matches the photon's energy, the radiation is more likely to be **transmitted**.
Free electrons in metals respond to low-frequency radiation, so metals **reflect** radio, microwaves and light.
If the photon energy is greater than the energy holding an electron, the atom can be **ionised**.

analogy.t: Ball games at a wall of nets
analogy.p: Imagine photons as balls thrown at a wall. Some walls are like a trampoline and bounce the ball back (reflection), some are like a net with big holes that lets the ball through (transmission), and some are like a sponge that soaks the ball up and wobbles (absorption, heating). A really fast ball (a high-frequency gamma photon) can knock a brick clean out of the wall - that is ionisation. Different balls behave differently at the same wall, just as wavelength decides what a material does. Where it breaks down: real photons are not tiny balls with a speed that changes; all photons travel at the same speed and differ in energy because of their frequency, and atoms can only absorb photons with exactly the right energy to make an electron jump between levels.

terms.d: When radiation bounces back off a surface.
When radiation passes through a material.
When radiation is taken in by a material, transferring its energy to the material.
The change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary between materials, caused by a change in speed.
The radiation arriving at a surface.
One of the fixed energies that an electron in an atom can have.
The giving out of radiation, for example when an electron falls to a lower energy level.
A packet of EM energy; its energy is proportional to the frequency of the radiation.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom; changes in unstable nuclei emit gamma rays.
Two or more atoms bonded together; molecular vibrations emit and absorb infrared.
An atom or molecule that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an overall charge.
The process of an atom or molecule losing (or gaining) electrons to become an ion.
Radiation with photons energetic enough to remove electrons from atoms: higher-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma rays.
Radiation whose photons have too little energy to ionise: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light.
The energy arriving per second per unit area.
A layer of the upper atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.

mistakes.w: Radiation that is absorbed disappears.
mistakes.r: Its energy is transferred to the absorbing material, usually heating it.

mistakes.w: X-rays bounce off bones.
mistakes.r: X-rays are absorbed by bone and transmitted by soft tissue.

mistakes.w: Any radiation can ionise if it is strong enough.
mistakes.r: Only radiation with high enough photon energy (high-frequency UV, X-rays, gamma) can ionise; intensity does not change the energy of each photon.

mistakes.w: Ionisation means an atom gains energy and gets hot.
mistakes.r: Ionisation means an electron is removed from an atom or molecule, leaving a charged ion.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are produced by electrons.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays are emitted by changes in the nucleus of unstable atoms.

mistakes.w: An electron emits a photon when it moves to a higher energy level.
mistakes.r: It absorbs a photon to move up and emits a photon when it falls to a lower level.

mistakes.w: Microwaves are ionising because they cook food.
mistakes.r: Microwaves are non-ionising; they are absorbed by water molecules and cause heating.

mistakes.w: A material either absorbs or transmits all EM radiation.
mistakes.r: What happens depends on the wavelength; for example glass transmits visible light but absorbs much UV.

exam.q: Name the process in which radiation passes through a material.
model: Transmission.
exam.tip: One-word answers must be the exact term.

exam.q: Which part of an atom emits gamma rays?
model: The nucleus.
exam.tip: Gamma = nucleus; X-rays, UV and visible = electrons.

exam.q: What is meant by ionisation?
model: An atom or molecule losing (or gaining) an electron to become a charged ion.
exam.tip: Mention electron removal and the word ion.

exam.q: Name two types of electromagnetic radiation that are ionising.
model: X-rays.
Gamma rays (or higher-frequency ultraviolet).
exam.tip: Any two of UV, X-ray, gamma.

exam.q: Explain why an X-ray image shows bones clearly.
model: X-rays are absorbed by bone.
X-rays are transmitted through soft tissue, so bones show as a shadow (white) on the detector.
exam.tip: Use absorbed and transmitted, not blocked and passes.

exam.q: Explain why a very bright red light cannot ionise atoms but a weak beam of gamma rays can.
model: Ionisation depends on the energy of each photon.
Red light has a low frequency so each photon has too little energy to remove an electron.
Gamma rays have a very high frequency, so each photon has enough energy to ionise; brightness only increases the number of photons.
exam.tip: Separate photon energy from intensity.

exam.q: Describe how an atom absorbs and then emits visible light.
model: An electron absorbs a photon of the right energy and moves to a higher energy level.
The electron later falls back to a lower energy level.
It emits a photon whose energy equals the difference between the levels.
exam.tip: Use the phrase energy level each time.

exam.q: A microwave oven heats food. Explain how, and why the metal walls of the oven are important.
model: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules in the food.
The energy is transferred to the molecules, so the food heats up.
Metal walls reflect the microwaves, keeping them inside the oven.
exam.tip: Name the process at each surface.

exam.q: Explain why ozone in the upper atmosphere is important for life on Earth.
model: Ozone absorbs most of the ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
This reduces the UV reaching the surface, which could ionise/damage cells and cause skin cancer.
exam.tip: Link absorption to reduced hazard.

exam.q: Describe how different types of electromagnetic radiation are emitted and absorbed by matter, and explain which types can ionise. Use examples from across the spectrum.
model: Radio waves are produced by oscillating currents in circuits and can induce currents when absorbed.
Infrared is emitted and absorbed by vibrating molecules; microwaves are absorbed by water molecules, causing heating.
Visible light and UV come from electrons changing energy levels in atoms.
X-rays come from inner electrons / fast electrons being stopped; gamma rays come from changes in the nucleus.
Larger energy changes give higher-frequency radiation with higher photon energy.
Higher-frequency UV, X-rays and gamma have enough photon energy to remove electrons (ionise); lower frequencies only cause heating.
exam.tip: Work through the spectrum in order so no region is missed.

worked.q: A hospital uses lead aprons and an X-ray machine. Explain, using the ideas of absorption and transmission, how an X-ray image is made and why staff stand behind a lead screen.
steps: X-rays are sent through the patient towards a detector.
Soft tissue transmits most X-rays, so they reach the detector and those areas look dark.
Bone absorbs X-rays, so fewer reach the detector behind bone, which looks white.
Lead is dense and absorbs X-rays strongly, so a lead screen stops X-rays reaching staff.
Staff are exposed many times a day, so reducing ionising radiation dose is important.
worked.ans: Images form because bone absorbs and soft tissue transmits X-rays; lead screens absorb X-rays to protect staff from repeated ionising doses.

worked.q: Sunlight shines through a glass window onto a desk. Describe what happens to the visible light and UV at the glass, and to the light at the desk.
steps: At the glass: some light is reflected (you can see faint reflections), most visible light is transmitted.
Much of the UV is absorbed by the glass, so less UV reaches the room.
At the desk: some light is reflected (so we can see the desk) and some is absorbed.
The absorbed energy heats the desk.
worked.ans: Glass reflects a little, transmits most visible light and absorbs much UV; the desk reflects some light and absorbs the rest, warming up.

phy_ocrb.0.2.summary: Every region of the EM spectrum has practical uses that depend on how it is absorbed, transmitted or reflected, from radio broadcasting to sterilising with gamma rays. The high-frequency regions, **ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays**, are hazardous to living tissue because their photons carry enough energy to **ionise** atoms and damage **DNA**, which can cause cell death, mutations and cancer. Radio waves are special because they can be **produced by alternating currents in electrical circuits**, and when absorbed by an aerial they **induce an alternating current of the same frequency**, which is how radio and TV transmission works.

core.p: The danger of EM radiation depends mainly on the **energy of each photon**, which rises with frequency. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have high enough frequencies to be **ionising**: they can knock electrons out of atoms in body tissue.
bullets: Ionisation creates reactive ions inside cells, which can break or change molecules.
Damage to **DNA** can cause **mutations**; cells may then divide uncontrollably, causing **cancer**.
Large doses can **kill cells** outright (radiation sickness, burns).
The risk increases with the **dose**: higher intensity and longer exposure mean more risk.
Lower-frequency radiation (radio, microwave, infrared) is non-ionising; its main hazard is heating if intense.

callouts.p: High frequency -> high-energy photons -> ionisation -> damage to DNA in cells -> mutations / cancer / cell death.

core.p: UV from the Sun and from sunbeds is absorbed by the **skin and eyes**. It does not penetrate deeply, so its damage is concentrated near the surface.
bullets: **Sunburn** - damage to skin cells.
**Premature skin ageing** (wrinkles).
**Skin cancer** - UV can damage DNA in skin cells.
**Eye damage**, including cataracts and damage to the cornea and retina.
Protection: sunscreen (absorbs UV), clothing, hats, sunglasses that absorb UV, limiting time in the Sun.
Dark skin contains more melanin, which absorbs UV and gives some protection, but does not make skin immune.

callouts.p: UV does not cause bones to break or mobile phone style heating. Its hazards are to skin and eyes.

core.h: Hazards of X-rays and gamma rays
core.p: X-rays and gamma rays are **very penetrating**: they pass into the body and can ionise atoms in cells deep inside, including internal organs.
bullets: They can **damage or kill cells** and cause **mutations** in DNA, increasing the risk of **cancer**.
Gamma rays have the highest photon energy and are the most penetrating.
Protection: **lead** shielding (aprons, screens), thick concrete, keeping distance, limiting exposure time.
Radiographers leave the room or stand behind a lead screen because they would otherwise receive many small doses every day.
The benefit of a medical X-ray or gamma treatment usually outweighs the small risk for the patient.

callouts.p: OCR often asks you to weigh up risk and benefit: a patient has one X-ray and gains a diagnosis; staff are shielded because they would face repeated exposure.

core.p: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths. They are transmitted through the atmosphere, through walls and can travel long distances, so they are ideal for **communication**.
bullets: **Radio and TV broadcasting**.
**Two-way radio** communication (emergency services, aircraft, ships).
Long-wavelength radio waves can diffract around hills and buildings.
Radio telescopes detect radio waves from space.
Uses depend on radio waves being transmitted through air and buildings without being absorbed.

core.p: Microwaves are shorter than radio waves. Some microwave frequencies pass straight through the atmosphere, while others are strongly absorbed by water.
bullets: **Satellite communication** and satellite TV - microwaves are transmitted through the atmosphere to satellites in space.
**Mobile phone** networks and Wi-Fi.
**Microwave ovens** - water molecules in food absorb the microwaves and heat up.
**Radar** - microwaves reflect from aircraft and ships to find their position and speed.
Weather forecasting satellites.

core.p: All warm objects emit infrared, and absorbing infrared causes heating. Hotter objects emit more.
bullets: **Cooking** (grills, toasters) and **electric heaters**.
**Thermal imaging cameras** - detect infrared emitted by warm bodies; used by police, firefighters, and to find heat loss from houses.
**Remote controls** for TVs.
**Optical fibre communication** - infrared pulses carry data along glass fibres.
Night-vision equipment and intruder alarms (passive infrared sensors).

core.p: Visible light is the only region our eyes detect, so it is used for seeing and anything involving images.
bullets: **Vision**, illumination and lighting.
**Photography** and video.
**Optical fibres** - visible light carries images in endoscopes used to see inside the body.
Lasers in barcode scanners and laser pointers.
Photosynthesis in plants depends on absorbing visible light.

core.p: Ultraviolet makes some chemicals **fluoresce** (absorb UV and emit visible light) and, because it can kill microorganisms, it is used for sterilising.
bullets: **Fluorescent lamps** and energy-efficient tubes - UV produced inside is absorbed by a coating that emits visible light.
**Security marking** - invisible ink glows under UV; banknote checks.
**Sterilising water** and killing bacteria.
**Sunbeds** and tanning (with the health risks above).
Detecting forged banknotes.

core.p: X-rays and gamma rays are very penetrating, and their ionising effect can be used deliberately to kill cells such as cancer cells or bacteria.
bullets: **X-rays: medical imaging** of bones and teeth - transmitted by soft tissue, absorbed by bone.
**X-rays: airport security scanners** to see inside luggage.
**X-rays and gamma: radiotherapy** - killing cancer cells.
**Gamma: sterilising** medical equipment and food - kills bacteria without heating, and works through sealed packaging.
**Gamma: medical tracers** - a gamma-emitting substance is followed through the body by a detector outside.

core.p: Radio waves are linked to electrical circuits in both directions. An **alternating current in a transmitter aerial** makes electrons oscillate, and **oscillating charges produce radio waves** with the **same frequency** as the current. When radio waves reach a receiving aerial, they are absorbed and make the electrons in it oscillate, **inducing an alternating current of the same frequency** in the receiver circuit.
bullets: **Transmitter**: a.c. in the circuit -> electrons oscillate up and down the aerial -> radio waves emitted.
**Receiver**: radio waves absorbed by the aerial -> electrons forced to oscillate -> a.c. induced in the circuit.
The induced a.c. has the **same frequency** as the radio wave (and as the transmitter current).
The signal (sound, pictures, data) is carried by changing (modulating) the radio wave; the receiver decodes the induced current.
Radio waves can be both **produced by** and **can themselves induce** oscillations in electrical circuits.
This only happens for low-frequency radiation like radio, because electrons in circuits can oscillate at these frequencies.

callouts.p: The alternating current induced in a receiving aerial has the same frequency as the radio waves that produced it.
Explaining radio waves and circuits is often a Higher tier question. Use the words oscillate, alternating current, induce and same frequency.

fig.cap: An alternating current in the transmitter makes electrons oscillate in its aerial, emitting radio waves; these induce an alternating current of the same frequency in the receiving aerial.

core.p: Many 6-mark questions ask you to explain why a particular region is used. Always link the use to a property.
bullets: Long-distance communication: needs radiation **transmitted** through the atmosphere (radio, microwaves).
Imaging inside the body: needs radiation **transmitted** by flesh but **absorbed** by bone (X-rays).
Killing cells: needs **ionising** and penetrating radiation (gamma).
Heating: needs radiation **absorbed** by the material (infrared, microwaves for water).
Avoid using ionising radiation where a safer option works.

analogy.p: Think of the EM spectrum as a toolbox. Radio waves are long-range walkie-talkies, microwaves are a cooking pot and satellite link, infrared is a warm blanket and a heat-seeing camera, visible light is your eyes, UV is a highlighter pen that makes things glow, and X-rays and gamma rays are a powerful drill that can see inside and even destroy - useful but dangerous if you point it at yourself. Each tool is chosen for what it does to materials. Where it breaks down: real tools do not get more dangerous in a smooth sequence, but EM radiation does: photon energy rises steadily with frequency, so the hazard depends on frequency, intensity and time of exposure, not on the job.

terms.d: Radiation whose photons have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms: UV, X-rays and gamma rays.
The molecule in cells that carries genetic information; damage to it can cause mutations.
A change in the DNA of a cell, which can lead to cancer.
Uncontrolled division of cells, which can be caused by DNA damage from ionising radiation.
A measure of the amount of radiation absorbed; risk increases with dose.
A cream that absorbs or reflects UV to reduce the amount reaching skin cells.
Absorbing UV and re-emitting the energy as visible light.
Killing bacteria and other microorganisms, for example with gamma rays or UV.
Using X-rays or gamma rays to kill cancer cells.
Forming an image from the infrared emitted by objects, showing their temperature.
A thin glass fibre that carries light or infrared signals by repeated total internal reflection.
A conductor used to emit or absorb radio waves.
Current that repeatedly changes direction; in an aerial it produces radio waves of the same frequency.
To cause a current or voltage in a conductor, for example by radio waves making electrons in an aerial oscillate.
A repeated back-and-forth motion, such as electrons moving up and down an aerial.
Detecting objects by reflecting microwaves or radio waves off them.

mistakes.w: Microwaves cause cancer because they are radiation.
mistakes.r: Microwaves are non-ionising; their hazard is heating. Cancer risk comes from ionising UV, X-rays and gamma rays.

mistakes.w: UV causes cancer of internal organs.
mistakes.r: UV is absorbed by the skin and eyes; it causes skin cancer, sunburn and eye damage.

mistakes.w: X-rays reflect off bones.
mistakes.r: X-rays are absorbed by bone and transmitted through soft tissue.

mistakes.w: Radiation kills cells by heating them up.
mistakes.r: Ionising radiation damages cells by ionising atoms and damaging DNA.

mistakes.w: Radio waves are sound waves that the aerial picks up.
mistakes.r: Radio waves are EM waves that induce an alternating current in the aerial; the circuit converts this signal to sound.

mistakes.w: The current in the receiver has a different frequency from the radio wave.
mistakes.r: The induced alternating current has the same frequency as the radio wave.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays make food radioactive when sterilising it.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays kill bacteria but do not make the food radioactive.

mistakes.w: A radiographer stays out of the room because one X-ray is very dangerous.
mistakes.r: They would receive many repeated doses each day; the risk builds with total dose.

exam.q: Give one use of gamma rays.
model: Sterilising medical equipment or food / killing cancer cells (radiotherapy) / medical tracers.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'sterilising surgical instruments' scores, 'medicine' may not.

exam.q: Name the type of EM radiation used in remote controls.
model: Infrared.
exam.tip: Common recall question.

exam.q: State two harmful effects of ultraviolet radiation on the human body.
model: Sunburn / premature skin ageing.
Skin cancer / eye damage such as cataracts.
exam.tip: Give two different effects, not two forms of the same one.

exam.q: Explain why gamma rays are used to sterilise surgical instruments.
model: Gamma rays are ionising and kill bacteria/microorganisms.
They are very penetrating so they pass through sealed packaging (and no heating is needed).
exam.tip: Link the use to two properties.

exam.q: Explain why X-rays can cause cancer but radio waves cannot.
model: X-rays have a much higher frequency so their photons carry more energy.
X-rays are ionising: they can remove electrons from atoms in cells.
This can damage DNA causing mutations/cancer; radio photons have too little energy to ionise.
exam.tip: Always name ionisation and DNA.

exam.q: Explain why satellite communication uses microwaves.
model: Microwaves (of the right frequency) are transmitted through the atmosphere.
So the signal can reach satellites in space and return to Earth.
exam.tip: The key property is transmission through the atmosphere.

exam.q: Describe how a microwave oven heats food.
model: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules in the food.
The energy transferred raises the temperature of the food.
exam.tip: Say absorbed by water molecules.

exam.q: A radiographer takes X-rays of patients. Explain why she stands behind a lead screen while the patient does not need one.
model: Lead absorbs X-rays.
The radiographer would be exposed many times a day, so her total dose would be large and the risk of cancer high.
The patient has only one or a few exposures, and the benefit of diagnosis outweighs the small risk.
exam.tip: Talk about dose and risk-benefit.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain how radio waves are produced by a transmitter and detected by a receiver.
model: An alternating current in the transmitter circuit makes electrons oscillate in the aerial.
The oscillating charges emit radio waves of the same frequency as the current.
The radio waves are absorbed by the receiving aerial and make its electrons oscillate.
This induces an alternating current in the receiver circuit with the same frequency as the radio waves.
exam.tip: Mention 'same frequency' at both ends.

exam.q: Compare the uses and hazards of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Explain why these three types are hazardous and what can be done to reduce the risk.
model: UV uses: fluorescent lamps, security marking, sterilising water; hazards: sunburn, skin cancer, eye damage.
X-ray uses: medical imaging, airport security; hazards: ionise and damage cells, cancer.
Gamma uses: sterilising, radiotherapy, tracers; hazards: kill cells, mutations, cancer.
All three have high frequency and high-energy photons that ionise atoms and damage DNA.
Risk increases with dose (intensity and time); X-rays and gamma are penetrating so affect internal organs.
Reduce risk: sunscreen/sunglasses/clothing for UV; lead shielding, distance and limited time for X-rays and gamma.
exam.tip: Structure it: uses, hazards, why, protection - for each of the three.

worked.q: A local radio station broadcasts at 95 MHz. What is the frequency of the alternating current induced in a car radio aerial tuned to this station, and why?
steps: Radio waves from the station make electrons in the car aerial oscillate.
The electrons are forced to oscillate at the frequency of the radio wave.
So the induced alternating current has the same frequency as the wave.
worked.ans: 95 MHz (9.5 x 10^7 Hz), because the induced a.c. has the same frequency as the radio waves that cause it.

worked.q: A company wants to sterilise sealed packs of syringes. They consider heating, UV light and gamma rays. Evaluate which is best.
steps: Heating could melt the plastic syringes, so it is unsuitable.
UV kills bacteria but is not very penetrating, so it would not get through the packaging reliably.
Gamma rays are ionising so they kill bacteria, and are very penetrating so they pass through sealed packs.
Gamma rays do not make the syringes radioactive; workers must be shielded with lead or concrete.
worked.ans: Gamma rays: they penetrate the sealed packaging and kill bacteria without heating, provided workers are shielded.

phy_ocrb.0.3.summary: **All objects emit electromagnetic radiation**, and both the **intensity** and the **range of wavelengths** emitted depend on temperature: hotter objects emit more radiation and their peak moves to **shorter wavelengths (higher frequencies)**. An object's temperature stays constant when it absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it; it warms if it absorbs faster and cools if it emits faster. The Earth's temperature is set by this **radiation balance**: the surface absorbs mainly visible light from the Sun and emits infrared, some of which is absorbed and re-emitted back by **greenhouse gases**, so increasing carbon dioxide from human activity is raising the global temperature.

core.p: Every object, whatever its temperature, emits electromagnetic radiation. The particles in an object are always moving and vibrating, and this emits radiation. Even ice and your body emit radiation, mostly as **infrared**.
bullets: **All objects emit and absorb** EM radiation all the time.
Cool objects (like people, around 37 C) emit mainly **infrared**, which we cannot see.
Very hot objects (a few thousand degrees) also emit **visible light** - they glow red, then yellow, then white as they get hotter.
The Sun (surface about 5500 C) emits mostly **visible light**, with infrared and ultraviolet too.
Thermal imaging cameras detect the infrared emitted by warm bodies.

callouts.p: All bodies emit radiation; the intensity and wavelength distribution of the emission depend on the temperature of the body.

core.h: How temperature changes the radiation emitted
core.p: Raising an object's temperature changes its radiation in two ways at once. OCR expects you to say both.
bullets: **Intensity increases**: a hotter object emits more energy per second at every wavelength.
**Peak shifts to shorter wavelength / higher frequency**: the wavelength at which most radiation is emitted gets shorter as temperature rises.
Each object emits a **spread (range) of wavelengths**, not a single one.
Example: an electric heater bar warms up - first it emits only infrared, then glows dull red, then bright orange as it gets hotter.
Stars: red stars are cooler, blue-white stars are hotter.

callouts.p: For 'how does the radiation from a hotter object differ', say: more intense (more radiation) AND peak at a shorter wavelength / higher frequency.

fig.cap: Intensity against wavelength for objects at three temperatures. The hotter object emits more at every wavelength, and its peak is at a shorter wavelength, closer to the visible band.

core.p: Exam questions often show intensity against wavelength (or frequency) curves for different temperatures. You need to interpret them.
bullets: The **area under the curve** represents the total power emitted - bigger for hotter objects.
The **peak** of the curve shows the wavelength at which the most radiation is emitted.
A hotter object's curve is **higher everywhere** and its peak is **further to the left** (on a wavelength axis).
On a **frequency** axis the hotter peak moves to the **right** (higher frequency) - check the axis!
The curves never cross: a hotter object emits more at every wavelength.

callouts.p: If the graph uses frequency, a hotter object's peak is at higher frequency (to the right). If it uses wavelength, the peak is to the left.

core.p: An object's temperature depends on the **balance between the radiation it absorbs and the radiation it emits**. Think of energy coming in and going out every second.
bullets: Absorbs **more** than it emits -> net energy gain -> **temperature rises**.
Emits **more** than it absorbs -> net energy loss -> **temperature falls**.
Absorbs **at the same rate** as it emits -> **temperature stays constant** (steady state / equilibrium).
As an object warms, it emits more radiation, so it eventually reaches a new, higher steady temperature where emission again equals absorption.
Everyday examples: a cup of tea cools until it emits at the same rate it absorbs from the room; a car in the Sun warms until it reaches a steady high temperature; a pavement cools on a clear night.

callouts.p: A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting it.
An object at constant temperature has not stopped emitting or absorbing - it is doing both at equal rates.

fig.cap: Radiation balance: if an object emits more than it absorbs it cools, if the two rates are equal its temperature stays steady, and if it absorbs more than it emits it warms up.

core.p: The type of surface affects how quickly an object absorbs and emits radiation.
bullets: **Matt black** surfaces are the **best absorbers and best emitters** of radiation.
**Shiny / white** surfaces are the **worst absorbers and emitters** - they **reflect** most radiation.
Good absorbers are also good emitters at the same temperature.
Uses: solar panels painted black to absorb; houses in hot countries painted white to reflect; shiny foil blankets for marathon runners and survival blankets reduce emission.
A matt black and a shiny can of hot water at the same start temperature: the matt black can cools faster.

core.h: Radiation from the Sun reaching the Earth
core.p: The Sun is very hot, so it emits mainly **visible light**, along with some ultraviolet and infrared. This radiation crosses space and reaches the Earth.
bullets: Some incoming radiation is **reflected** back to space by clouds, ice and snow.
Some is **absorbed** by the atmosphere (UV by the ozone layer, some IR).
Most visible light is **transmitted** through the atmosphere and is **absorbed by the Earth's surface**, warming it.
The amount absorbed depends on surface: ice reflects strongly, oceans and forests absorb strongly.

core.p: The Earth's surface is much cooler than the Sun, so it emits radiation of **lower frequency (longer wavelength)**: mainly **infrared**.
bullets: Earth's surface average temperature is about 15 C, so its emission peaks in the **infrared**.
This IR is emitted upwards towards space.
The difference matters: the atmosphere transmits most incoming **visible** light but absorbs much of the outgoing **infrared**.
This is the key to the greenhouse effect.

callouts.p: Radiation in from the hot Sun is mostly visible (short wavelength); radiation out from the cool Earth is infrared (longer wavelength).

core.p: Some gases in the atmosphere, called **greenhouse gases**, are transparent to visible light but **absorb infrared**. They then **re-emit** this infrared in all directions, including back towards the Earth's surface. This keeps the Earth warmer than it would be with no atmosphere.
bullets: Main greenhouse gases: **carbon dioxide (CO2)**, **water vapour** and **methane**.
Step 1: visible light from the Sun is transmitted through the atmosphere and absorbed by the surface.
Step 2: the warmed surface emits infrared.
Step 3: greenhouse gases **absorb** some of this infrared.
Step 4: they **re-emit** infrared in all directions; some goes **back to the surface**, warming it further.
The Earth reaches a steady temperature when the total energy radiated to space equals the energy absorbed from the Sun.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth's average temperature would be about -18 C, too cold for most life.

callouts.p: The warming of the Earth's surface because greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared emitted by the surface and re-emit some of it back towards the Earth.

callouts.t: Not a hole in the ozone
callouts.p: The greenhouse effect is about infrared being absorbed by gases such as CO2. It is NOT caused by the ozone hole, and it does not involve heat being 'trapped' by reflection.

core.h: Increasing carbon dioxide and global warming
core.p: Human activities are increasing the amount of carbon dioxide (and methane) in the atmosphere. More greenhouse gas absorbs more infrared, so less escapes to space and the radiation balance shifts: the Earth absorbs more than it emits until it warms to a new, higher temperature.
bullets: **Burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, gas) in power stations, vehicles and homes releases CO2.
**Deforestation** - fewer trees remove CO2 by photosynthesis, and burning forests releases CO2.
Methane is released from cattle farming, rice paddies and landfill.
Atmospheric CO2 has risen from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution to over 400 ppm today.
**Evidence of warming**: records show the global average temperature has risen by about 1 C since the late 1800s; scientists see the correlation between rising CO2 and rising temperature.
Scientists use **computer models** to predict future temperature change; most agree human activity is the main cause of recent warming.

callouts.p: A graph showing CO2 and temperature rising together shows a correlation. To argue cause, explain the mechanism: more CO2 absorbs more infrared and re-emits it back to Earth.

core.p: A higher average global temperature has many knock-on effects. Questions may ask you to suggest some.
bullets: **Melting ice sheets and glaciers**, and expansion of warmer sea water, leading to **rising sea levels** and flooding of low-lying land.
**Changes to weather patterns** and climate: more extreme weather, droughts, heavy rainfall and storms.
Changes to where crops can grow and to habitats, affecting wildlife.
Melting ice reveals darker ground and sea, which absorb more radiation - a feedback that speeds up warming.
Ways to reduce it: use renewable energy, improve energy efficiency, reduce deforestation, plant trees.

core.p: A full answer on the Earth's temperature links the ideas of emission, absorption and balance in a chain.
bullets: Sun is hot -> emits mostly visible light.
Atmosphere transmits visible -> surface absorbs -> surface warms.
Surface is cooler -> emits infrared (longer wavelength).
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared -> re-emit some back to the surface.
More greenhouse gas -> less infrared escapes -> Earth absorbs more than it emits -> temperature rises until a new balance is reached.

analogy.t: A bath with the tap on and the plug out
analogy.p: The Earth's temperature is like the water level in a bath with the tap running and the plug out. The tap is the radiation absorbed from the Sun; the plughole is the infrared radiated to space. The level stays steady when water flows in and out at the same rate. Adding greenhouse gas is like partly blocking the plughole: water drains more slowly, so the level rises - but as it rises, the pressure pushes water out faster, until a new, higher steady level is reached. Where it breaks down: in a real bath the blocked water just stays put, but greenhouse gases do not store the infrared - they absorb it and re-emit it in all directions, some back down to the surface; and the radiation coming in (visible) is a different type from what goes out (infrared).

terms.d: The giving out of electromagnetic radiation by an object.
The taking in of radiation by an object, transferring energy to it.
The energy arriving per second per unit area; hotter objects emit radiation of greater intensity.
The spread of wavelengths emitted by an object and how much is emitted at each one.
The wavelength at which an object emits the most radiation; it gets shorter as temperature rises.
EM radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light; emitted by all warm objects.
The comparison between the rate at which a body absorbs radiation and the rate at which it emits it.
When a body absorbs and emits radiation at the same rate, so its temperature stays constant.
A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour that absorbs infrared radiation.
Warming of the Earth's surface because greenhouse gases absorb infrared from the surface and re-emit some back.
The increase in the Earth's average surface temperature, linked to increased greenhouse gases from human activity.
Coal, oil and natural gas; burning them releases carbon dioxide.
Cutting down or burning forests, which reduces CO2 removal and releases CO2.
Long-term changes to weather patterns, caused by global warming.
A link in which two variables change together; does not by itself prove one causes the other.
A computer simulation used by scientists to predict how the climate will change.

mistakes.w: Only hot objects emit radiation.
mistakes.r: All objects emit radiation; the intensity and wavelengths depend on temperature.

mistakes.w: A hotter object emits radiation of longer wavelength.
mistakes.r: A hotter object emits more intense radiation with its peak at a shorter wavelength (higher frequency).

mistakes.w: An object at constant temperature has stopped emitting radiation.
mistakes.r: It is absorbing and emitting at the same rate.

mistakes.w: Greenhouse gases reflect heat back to Earth.
mistakes.r: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back to the surface.

mistakes.w: The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
mistakes.r: The ozone layer absorbs UV; the greenhouse effect is due to gases like CO2 absorbing infrared.

mistakes.w: Greenhouse gases absorb the incoming sunlight.
mistakes.r: They transmit most incoming visible light but absorb the outgoing infrared from the cooler Earth.

mistakes.w: The greenhouse effect is bad and should be stopped.
mistakes.r: The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life; the problem is the enhanced effect from extra CO2.

mistakes.w: The Earth emits the same type of radiation as the Sun.
mistakes.r: The Earth is much cooler so it emits mainly infrared, of longer wavelength than the Sun's mostly visible radiation.

exam.q: Which objects emit electromagnetic radiation?
model: All objects (at any temperature).
exam.tip: Do not limit it to hot objects.

exam.q: Name one greenhouse gas.
model: Carbon dioxide / methane / water vapour.
exam.tip: Oxygen and nitrogen are not greenhouse gases.

exam.q: Describe two ways the radiation from an object changes as its temperature increases.
model: The intensity (amount) of radiation emitted increases.
The peak wavelength becomes shorter / peak frequency becomes higher.
exam.tip: Always give both: more intense AND shorter peak wavelength.

exam.q: A cup of hot tea is left in a room. Its temperature falls and then stays constant. Explain this in terms of radiation.
model: At first the tea emits radiation faster than it absorbs it, so it cools.
As it cools, it emits less radiation.
When it is absorbing and emitting at the same rate (room temperature), its temperature stays constant.
exam.tip: Use 'rate' and compare absorbing with emitting.

exam.q: Explain why radiation emitted by the Earth has a longer wavelength than radiation emitted by the Sun.
model: The Earth is much cooler than the Sun.
Cooler objects emit radiation with a peak at longer wavelength (infrared rather than visible).
exam.tip: Link temperature to peak wavelength.

exam.q: A graph shows the intensity of radiation against wavelength for two stars, A and B. The curve for A is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength. Which star is hotter? Give two reasons.
model: Star A is hotter.
It emits radiation with greater intensity (higher curve).
Its peak is at a shorter wavelength.
exam.tip: Quote both features of the graph.

exam.q: Explain why the matt black panels of a solar water heater heat up faster than shiny panels.
model: Matt black surfaces are good absorbers of radiation.
Shiny surfaces reflect most of the radiation, so absorb less.
exam.tip: Compare absorbing with reflecting.

exam.q: Give two human activities that increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
model: Burning fossil fuels (power stations, cars).
Deforestation / burning forests.
exam.tip: Be specific about the activity.

exam.q: Suggest two possible consequences of an increase in the Earth's average temperature.
model: Melting ice / rising sea levels / flooding.
More extreme weather / changes in climate / effects on crops and habitats.
exam.tip: Give two distinct consequences.

exam.q: Explain how the Earth's temperature is determined by the radiation it absorbs and emits, and why increasing carbon dioxide levels cause the Earth's temperature to rise.
model: The Sun is very hot and emits mainly visible light (short wavelength), which is transmitted by the atmosphere.
The Earth's surface absorbs this radiation and warms up.
The Earth is cooler so emits mainly infrared (longer wavelength).
Greenhouse gases such as CO2 absorb some of this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back towards the surface.
Earth's temperature is constant when it radiates energy to space at the same rate as it absorbs from the Sun.
More CO2 absorbs more infrared, so less escapes; the Earth absorbs more than it emits and warms until a new, higher balance temperature is reached.
exam.tip: Follow the energy path in order: in, absorbed, out, absorbed and re-emitted, balance, change.

worked.q: Apply the idea of radiation balance: a car is parked in strong sunshine. Explain why its temperature rises and then levels off at a high value.
steps: At first the car absorbs radiation from the Sun faster than it emits radiation, so its temperature rises.
As the car gets hotter, it emits radiation at a greater rate (more intense).
Eventually the rate of emission equals the rate of absorption.
Then the temperature stays constant at this high steady value.
worked.ans: The temperature rises while absorption exceeds emission, then levels off when emission has risen to match absorption.

worked.q: Two cans, one matt black and one shiny silver, are filled with water at 80 C and left to cool. Predict and explain which cools faster.
steps: Both cans emit infrared because they are hotter than the room.
Matt black surfaces are better emitters than shiny surfaces.
So the matt black can emits radiation at a greater rate.
It loses energy faster, so its temperature falls faster.
worked.ans: The matt black can cools faster because it is the better emitter of infrared.

worked.q: Data show atmospheric CO2 rose from 315 ppm in 1960 to 415 ppm in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase and explain why scientists link this to warming.
steps: Increase = 415 - 315 = 100 ppm.
Percentage increase = 100 / 315 x 100 = 31.7%.
Over the same period global temperature also rose: a correlation.
Mechanism: more CO2 absorbs more infrared emitted by the Earth and re-emits some back, so the Earth absorbs more than it emits and warms.
worked.ans: About a 32% increase; it is linked to warming because of the correlation and the known infrared absorption mechanism.

phy_ocrb.0.4.summary: A wave is a regular disturbance that **transfers energy** from one place to another **without transferring matter**. Every wave can be described by its **amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period**, and these quantities can be read from displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs. Waves are either **transverse** (oscillations at right angles to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. ripples on water and all electromagnetic waves) or **longitudinal** (oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound), and you must be able to describe evidence that it is the wave, not the medium, that travels.

core.p: A wave is a travelling disturbance. The particles of the medium (or the electric and magnetic fields, for EM waves) **oscillate about a fixed rest position**, passing energy on to their neighbours. The pattern moves forward but each particle ends up back where it started, so **energy and information are transferred but matter is not**.
bullets: Mechanical waves (water ripples, sound, waves on a string or slinky) need a **medium** to travel through.
Electromagnetic waves do not need a medium and can travel through a vacuum.
An **oscillation** is a repeated back-and-forth (or up-and-down) movement about a rest position.
Waves can carry information as well as energy, e.g. radio signals, sound in speech.
The **medium** is the material the wave travels through, e.g. water, air, a spring.

callouts.p: A wave transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.

core.h: Evidence that the wave travels, not the medium
core.p: OCR asks you to describe evidence that it is the wave and not the water or air that moves. The classic observations all show an object or particle bobbing in place while the wave pattern moves past it.
bullets: A **cork or duck floating on ripples** moves up and down but does not travel along with the ripples.
In a ripple tank, a small float stays in roughly the same place as ripples pass.
A **ribbon tied to a slinky** moves back and forth (longitudinal) or up and down (transverse) but stays at the same point along the slinky.
Sound from a loudspeaker reaches you, but the air in front of the speaker is not blown across the room into your ear: air particles only vibrate.
If matter travelled with the wave, the floating object would be carried away from the source.

callouts.p: Name the object (cork, ribbon), say what it does (oscillates up and down / back and forth) and what it does NOT do (it does not move along with the wave).

core.p: The amplitude is the **maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its rest (undisturbed) position**. It is measured from the middle line to the top of a crest or the bottom of a trough, **never crest to trough**.
bullets: Units: metres (m), or cm / mm on small diagrams.
A larger amplitude means the wave carries **more energy**.
For sound, larger amplitude means a **louder** sound.
For water waves, larger amplitude means taller waves.
Amplitude does not affect the wave speed or the frequency.

callouts.p: The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.
Crest to trough distance is TWICE the amplitude. Halve it.

fig.cap: A transverse wave drawn as displacement against distance. Amplitude is measured from the rest position to a crest; wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next (or between any two matching points).

core.p: The wavelength (symbol lambda) is the **distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave**, for example crest to crest, trough to trough, or compression to compression.
bullets: Units: metres (m).
It can only be read from a **displacement-distance** graph (the x-axis is distance).
On a longitudinal wave, wavelength = distance between the centres of two neighbouring compressions (or rarefactions).
Measure across several wavelengths and divide, to reduce the uncertainty in the measurement.
Two points one whole wavelength apart are moving in step (in phase).

callouts.p: The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.

core.p: Frequency is the **number of waves passing a fixed point per second**, which is the same as the number of complete oscillations each particle makes per second. It is set by the **source** of the wave and does not change when the wave enters a new medium.
bullets: Units: **hertz (Hz)**. 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.
kHz = 1000 Hz; MHz = 1 000 000 Hz; GHz = 10^9 Hz.
For sound, higher frequency means a **higher pitch**.
For light, frequency determines colour.
Frequency is decided by how fast the source vibrates, e.g. a dipper in a ripple tank or a loudspeaker cone.

callouts.p: The number of waves passing a point each second (measured in hertz, Hz).

core.h: Period and the link to frequency
core.p: The period T is the **time taken for one complete wave to pass a point**, or for one particle to make one complete oscillation. Because frequency counts waves per second and period is seconds per wave, they are **reciprocals** of each other.
bullets: Equation: **period = 1 / frequency**, T = 1 / f.
Rearranged: f = 1 / T.
Units: period in seconds (s), frequency in hertz (Hz).
A high frequency means a short period: if 50 waves pass per second, each takes 1/50 = 0.02 s.
Period is read from a **displacement-time** graph (the x-axis is time), as the time between two crests.

callouts.p: T = 1 / f. Convert kHz or ms to Hz and s before substituting.

fig.cap: A displacement-time graph for one point on a wave. The time between neighbouring crests is the period T; frequency is 1 divided by T.

core.p: Exam questions often give a graph and ask you to read off amplitude, wavelength or period. **Always check the x-axis label first**: distance means you can find wavelength; time means you can find period (and so frequency).
bullets: Both types of graph show amplitude on the y-axis.
Displacement-distance graph: a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant.
Displacement-time graph: the motion of one point over time.
Count the number of complete waves across the graph and divide the total distance or time by that number.
Check the scale on each axis and the units (cm, ms).

callouts.p: Do not read a 'wavelength' off a graph whose x-axis is time: that length is the period.

core.p: In a transverse wave the oscillations are **perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction in which the wave transfers energy**. The wave has peaks called **crests** and dips called **troughs**.
bullets: Examples: **ripples on the surface of water**, waves on a string or rope, a slinky shaken side to side, and **all electromagnetic waves** (light, radio, X-rays etc).
S-waves (secondary seismic waves) are also transverse.
A transverse wave on a slinky is made by moving one end side to side across the direction of the slinky.
Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields rather than moving particles, so they can travel through a vacuum.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

fig.cap: In a transverse wave the oscillation (red arrows) is at right angles to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave it is parallel to it.

core.p: In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are **parallel to the direction in which the wave transfers energy**. Particles bunch together in **compressions** (high pressure) and spread apart in **rarefactions** (low pressure).
bullets: Examples: **sound waves** in air, liquids and solids, a slinky pushed and pulled along its length, and **P-waves** (primary seismic waves).
A longitudinal wave needs a medium, which is why **sound cannot travel through a vacuum**.
Compressions and rarefactions travel along; the particles only move back and forth about their rest positions.
Wavelength = distance between the centres of adjacent compressions.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

fig.cap: A longitudinal wave on a slinky. Coils crowd together at compressions and spread apart at rarefactions while each coil vibrates back and forth along the direction of energy transfer.
