core.p: Both types transfer energy without transferring matter and both have amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. The difference is the **direction of the oscillation compared with the direction of energy transfer**.
bullets: Transverse: crests and troughs.
Longitudinal: compressions and rarefactions.
Both obey wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
Only transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves need a medium; EM waves (transverse) do not.

callouts.p: Always say 'compared with the direction of energy transfer' (or 'direction of travel'). 'Up and down' alone does not score.

core.p: A slinky spring is used in class to model both kinds of wave, which is why OCR likes questions about it. The same spring can carry either type depending on how the end is moved.
bullets: Move the end **side to side**, across the spring: transverse wave.
Push and pull the end **along the length** of the spring: longitudinal wave.
Moving the hand faster increases the frequency and so shortens the wavelength (the speed in the spring stays about the same).
Moving the hand further increases the amplitude.
A piece of tape on one coil shows the coil oscillates but does not travel along the spring.

core.p: Amplitude is independent of the other three; wavelength, frequency and period are linked. If the wave speed in a medium is fixed, **increasing the frequency shortens the wavelength**, because more waves have to fit into the same distance travelled each second.
bullets: Frequency and period: f = 1 / T.
Wave speed links frequency and wavelength (covered in the next spec point): v = f x lambda.
Energy carried depends on amplitude (and, for EM radiation, on frequency).
Changing amplitude does not change frequency, period or wavelength.

callouts.p: Frequency is fixed by the source; amplitude by how much energy the source puts in.

analogy.t: A Mexican wave in a stadium
analogy.p: In a Mexican wave each fan stands up and sits down in their own seat, but the 'wave' races round the stadium. The fans are the particles of the medium, standing and sitting is the oscillation, and the moving pattern is the wave carrying energy. Because fans move up and down while the wave moves sideways, this is a transverse wave; if each fan instead leant left and right along the row, bunching into neighbours, it would model a longitudinal wave. It breaks down because fans choose when to move (each particle is pushed by its neighbour, not reacting to what it sees), and nothing like it can model an EM wave, which needs no medium at all.

terms.d: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A repeated movement back and forth about a fixed rest position.
The material through which a wave travels, such as water, air or a spring.
The undisturbed position of a particle when no wave is passing.
The distance of a point on the wave from its rest position, in a particular direction.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest position.
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, in metres.
The number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, in seconds; T = 1 / f.
The unit of frequency: one wave or oscillation per second.
A wave whose oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave whose oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
The highest point of a transverse wave (maximum positive displacement).
The lowest point of a transverse wave (maximum negative displacement).
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are closest together (higher pressure).
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are furthest apart (lower pressure).

mistakes.w: Amplitude is the distance from crest to trough.
mistakes.r: Amplitude is from the rest position to a crest (or to a trough): half the crest-to-trough height.

mistakes.w: Waves transfer particles / water moves along with the wave.
mistakes.r: Waves transfer energy (and information) but not matter; particles oscillate about fixed positions.

mistakes.w: In a transverse wave the particles move up and down.
mistakes.r: The oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (wave travel).

mistakes.w: Sound is a transverse wave.
mistakes.r: Sound is longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

mistakes.w: Frequency is how fast the wave travels.
mistakes.r: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second; speed is distance travelled per second.

mistakes.w: Reading wavelength from a displacement-time graph.
mistakes.r: A displacement-time graph gives the period; wavelength needs a displacement-distance graph.

mistakes.w: Wavelength measured from a crest to the next trough.
mistakes.r: Wavelength is crest to crest (or between any two equivalent adjacent points); crest to trough is half a wavelength.

mistakes.w: Period = frequency x 1 s, or forgetting to convert ms.
mistakes.r: T = 1 / f with f in Hz and T in s; convert ms to s and kHz to Hz first.

exam.q: State what is transferred by a wave.
model: Energy (or information); not matter.
exam.tip: Mentioning that matter is not transferred makes the answer secure.

exam.q: Define the frequency of a wave and give its unit.
model: Number of waves passing a point per second.
Hertz (Hz).
exam.tip: 'Per second' is essential.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a transverse and a longitudinal wave.
model: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer.
Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer.
exam.tip: Compare the oscillation with the direction of energy transfer in both halves.

exam.q: Give one example of a transverse wave and one example of a longitudinal wave.
model: Transverse: water ripples / any EM wave (e.g. light) / S-wave.
Longitudinal: sound / P-wave.
exam.tip: Avoid vague answers like 'a wave in the sea'; say ripples on water.

exam.q: A duck floats on a pond. Ripples pass it. Describe how the duck moves and explain what this shows about waves.
model: The duck bobs up and down but does not move along with the ripples.
This shows the wave transfers energy but not the water (matter).
exam.tip: Describe then explain: two separate marks.

exam.q: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz. Calculate its period.
exam.tip: Show the equation; give units.

exam.q: The period of a sound wave is 2.5 ms. Calculate its frequency.
model: f = 400 Hz
exam.tip: Convert ms to s first or you will be out by 1000.

exam.q: A displacement-distance graph of a water wave shows 4 complete waves across 1.2 m. The distance from a crest to a trough, measured vertically, is 6 cm. Determine the wavelength and amplitude.
model: Wavelength = 1.2 / 4 = 0.30 m
Crest-to-trough 6 cm is twice the amplitude
Amplitude = 3 cm (0.03 m)
exam.tip: Halve crest-to-trough for amplitude.

exam.q: Describe how a slinky spring can be used to show both transverse and longitudinal waves, and how to show that the spring itself does not travel with the wave.
model: Move one end side to side (perpendicular to the spring) for a transverse wave.
Push and pull one end along the length of the spring for a longitudinal wave.
Attach a ribbon or tape to one coil.
The ribbon oscillates about one position but does not move along the spring.
exam.tip: Give direction of hand movement relative to the spring's length.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how a sound wave travels through air. Use the words compression and rarefaction.
model: The loudspeaker cone vibrates, pushing and pulling air particles.
Particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer (longitudinal).
Regions where particles are close together are compressions; spread out are rarefactions.
Particles pass energy to neighbours; the compressions/rarefactions move, but the particles only vibrate about fixed positions.
exam.tip: State clearly that air does not flow from speaker to ear.

exam.q: A student says that increasing the amplitude of a water wave increases its frequency and wavelength. Evaluate this claim, explaining what each quantity depends on.
model: The claim is wrong.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from rest; it depends on energy given by the source.
Larger amplitude means more energy carried (taller waves).
Frequency is set by how many times per second the source vibrates, so it is unchanged by amplitude.
Wave speed depends on the medium (e.g. water depth), so it is unchanged.
Since v = f x lambda with v and f unchanged, wavelength is unchanged too.
exam.tip: For 6 marks, link each quantity to what controls it and reach a clear conclusion.

worked.q: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Calculate the period of the waves.
steps: Use T = 1 / f.

worked.q: A displacement-time graph for a point on a wave shows 5 complete oscillations in 0.20 s, with crests at +4 mm. Find the amplitude, period and frequency.
steps: Amplitude = maximum displacement from rest = 4 mm.
Period = total time / number of oscillations = 0.20 / 5 = 0.04 s.
Frequency = 1 / T = 1 / 0.04 = 25 Hz.
Check: 5 oscillations in 0.2 s = 25 per second. Consistent.
worked.ans: Amplitude 4 mm, period 0.04 s, frequency 25 Hz.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why sound cannot travel through space but light can.
steps: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave: it travels by particles vibrating and passing energy to neighbouring particles.
Space is a vacuum, so there are no particles to vibrate.
Light is an electromagnetic (transverse) wave made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which need no medium.
So light from the Sun reaches Earth but sound from it does not.
worked.ans: Sound needs a medium of particles; light is an EM wave that can travel through a vacuum.

phy_ocrb.0.5.summary: The speed of any wave is linked to its frequency and wavelength by **wave speed = frequency x wavelength** (v = f x lambda), and also by the general rule **speed = distance / time**. You must be able to use and rearrange the wave equation with correct units and prefixes, and describe how to **measure the speed of ripples on water using a ripple tank (PAG4)** and the **speed of sound in air**, choosing methods that reduce uncertainty. The speed depends on the **medium**, while the frequency is fixed by the source, so in a given medium a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

core.p: Each second the source makes f waves, and each wave is lambda metres long, so the front of the wave moves f x lambda metres every second. That distance per second is the **wave speed**.
bullets: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m)**
Symbols: v = f x lambda.
Rearranged: f = v / lambda and lambda = v / f.
This applies to all waves: water, sound, waves on strings and electromagnetic waves.
It is on the OCR equation sheet, but you must be able to recall and apply it.

callouts.p: wave speed = frequency x wavelength. Units must be m/s, Hz and m.

core.p: A wave crest is just something moving at a steady speed, so you can also find the wave speed by timing how long a crest takes to travel a measured distance. This is the basis of most practical methods.
bullets: **speed (m/s) = distance (m) / time (s)**
Use it when you know how far a wave has gone and how long it took (e.g. echoes, timing a ripple across a tank).
Use v = f x lambda when you know frequency and wavelength.
Both should give the same answer for the same wave: comparing them is a good check.

core.p: Most lost marks on wave calculations come from prefixes. Convert to base units before substituting.
bullets: kHz x 1000 = Hz; MHz x 10^6 = Hz; GHz x 10^9 = Hz.
Use standard form for EM waves, e.g. 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
Give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures (same as the data, usually 2 or 3).

callouts.p: Wavelength in cm with speed in m/s gives an answer 100 times too big. Convert cm to m first.

core.h: What controls wave speed, frequency and wavelength
core.p: The **speed of a wave depends on the medium** it travels through. The **frequency is set by the source**. Wavelength then adjusts so that v = f x lambda is true.
bullets: In a ripple tank, water waves travel **slower in shallower water**.
Sound travels at about **330 to 340 m/s in air**, about 1500 m/s in water and several thousand m/s in solids such as steel.
All EM waves travel at **3.0 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum**.
If the frequency of the source is doubled while the medium stays the same, the speed is unchanged so the **wavelength halves**.
Amplitude does not affect wave speed.

callouts.p: Speed depends on the medium; frequency depends on the source; wavelength follows from both.

core.p: A ripple tank is a shallow glass-bottomed tray of water. A **motor-driven dipper or straight bar** touches the surface and makes regular ripples at a known frequency. A **lamp above** shines through the water and the ripples act like lenses, casting bright and dark lines onto **white paper or a screen below**, so the wavefronts can be seen and measured.
bullets: A straight bar makes **straight (plane) wavefronts**; a point dipper makes circular ones.
The frequency is set by the motor speed on the power supply.
Keep the water depth constant (about 5 to 10 mm) so the speed is the same everywhere.
Ensure the tank is level, otherwise the depth and speed vary across it.
Each bright line on the screen is a crest; the gap between neighbouring bright lines is one wavelength (as projected).

core.h: PAG4: measuring wavelength in the ripple tank
core.p: Individual waves are small and moving, so measure **across several wavelengths** and divide. This reduces the percentage uncertainty in the measurement.
bullets: Place a **ruler on the paper** next to the projected pattern.
Take a **photograph** (or video) of the pattern with the ruler in shot, so the waves can be 'frozen'.
Count, say, 10 wavelengths and measure the total length L; wavelength = L / 10.
Alternatively use a **stroboscope** set to the wave frequency so the waves appear stationary.
Note: the shadow pattern is slightly magnified compared with the real waves; for a fair result the ruler can be placed in the water or the magnification measured.

callouts.p: 'Measure several wavelengths and divide by the number of waves' is a common mark for reducing uncertainty.

core.h: PAG4: measuring frequency and speed of ripples
core.p: With wavelength and frequency known, use v = f x lambda. Speed can also be found directly with speed = distance / time.
bullets: **Frequency method 1:** count the number of waves passing a point in a measured time (e.g. 10 s) and divide by the time.
**Frequency method 2:** read the frequency from the power supply / signal generator, or use a stroboscope.
**Direct speed method:** time how long one wavefront takes to travel the length of the tank (measured with a ruler); speed = distance / time.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean; identify and discard anomalies.
Video at a known frame rate allows timing more precisely than a stopwatch.

callouts.p: Timing a single ripple with a stopwatch has a large uncertainty from human reaction time (about 0.2 s). Time over a long distance or many waves.

core.h: Ripple tank: variables, errors and safety
core.p: A good PAG answer names the independent, dependent and control variables and explains how to make results more accurate.
bullets: Independent variable: e.g. frequency of the motor or depth of water.
Dependent: wavelength or speed.
Control: water depth (when changing frequency), tank level, same measuring method.
Random error: reaction time, judging moving lines; reduce by repeats and measuring many waves.
Safety: water near a mains lamp and power supply, wipe up spills; do not look directly at a bright lamp.

core.h: Measuring the speed of sound in air: echo method
core.p: Stand a measured distance (e.g. 50 m or more) from a large flat wall. Clap and listen for the echo, which has travelled **to the wall and back, a total distance of 2d**.
bullets: Measure the distance d to the wall with a **trundle wheel or long tape measure**.
Clap repeatedly so each clap coincides with the echo of the previous one; time e.g. 20 claps.
Time per round trip = total time / number of intervals.
Speed = 2d / time for one round trip.
Use a large distance so the time is long compared with reaction time.

callouts.p: Forgetting the factor of 2: the echo travels there AND back.

core.h: Measuring the speed of sound: other methods
core.p: Electronic timing removes human reaction time and so gives much more accurate values.
bullets: **Two microphones and a timer/oscilloscope:** place two microphones a measured distance apart in line with a sound; the timer starts when the first detects the sound and stops when the second does; speed = distance / time.

**Oscilloscope wavelength method:** a speaker connected to a signal generator plays a known frequency; move one microphone until the two traces are back in step; the distance moved is one wavelength; v = f x lambda.
**Distant event method:** watch someone bang cymbals or fire a starting pistol a long way away (e.g. 500 m); start timing on seeing it (light arrives almost instantly) and stop on hearing it.
Datalogger and sound sensors can also be used.

fig.cap: Two microphones connected to an oscilloscope. Moving microphone B away from A until the traces line up again moves it one wavelength; then wave speed = frequency x wavelength.

core.h: Choosing a method and judging data
core.p: Questions often give results and ask which is more accurate or why values differ from the accepted 340 m/s. Link the size of the measurement to the size of the uncertainty.
bullets: A longer time or distance gives a smaller **percentage uncertainty**.
Electronic timing is more precise than a stopwatch.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random error.
Wind and temperature change the speed of sound measured outdoors.
Results close together are precise; results close to the true value are accurate.

analogy.p: Imagine a band where each musician takes f steps per second and each step is lambda metres long. The band moves forward at f x lambda metres per second, just like a wave. If the ground changes to mud (a new medium), the band must slow down; if the drummer keeps the same beat (frequency fixed by the source), each step must get shorter (smaller wavelength). It breaks down because the musicians really do travel forward, whereas in a wave the particles stay in place and only the energy moves.

terms.d: The distance travelled by a wave (e.g. a crest) per second, in m/s.
wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda).
The number of waves passing a point per second, in hertz (Hz).
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, in m.
The material a wave travels through; it determines the wave speed.
A shallow transparent tray of water with a vibrating dipper, used to produce and observe water waves.
The part touching the water in a ripple tank that oscillates to produce ripples at a set frequency.
A line joining points on a wave that are at the same point in their cycle, e.g. along a crest.
A flashing light; when its flash frequency matches the wave frequency the waves appear to stand still.
A reflected sound wave heard after the original sound.
A wheel that clicks every metre, used to measure long distances outdoors.
A device that displays electrical signals (e.g. from microphones) as traces against time.
The range within which the true value of a measurement is likely to lie.
Unpredictable variation between repeat readings, e.g. from reaction time; reduced by repeating and averaging.
How close a measured value is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.

mistakes.w: Echo: speed = d / t using distance to the wall.
mistakes.r: The sound travels to the wall and back: speed = 2d / t.

mistakes.w: Substituting wavelength in cm or frequency in kHz directly.
mistakes.r: Convert to m and Hz first so the speed is in m/s.

mistakes.w: Increasing frequency increases wave speed.
mistakes.r: Speed depends on the medium; increasing frequency decreases wavelength at the same speed.

mistakes.w: Measure one wavelength to make it accurate.
mistakes.r: Measure across several wavelengths and divide, to reduce uncertainty.

mistakes.w: Time the sound with a stopwatch over a short distance.
mistakes.r: Use a large distance or electronic timing (two microphones) to reduce the effect of reaction time.

mistakes.w: Repeating readings makes the results more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of random error and lets anomalies be spotted; it improves precision/reliability.

mistakes.w: lambda = f / v.
mistakes.r: lambda = v / f.

mistakes.w: Using a light flash and sound together: start timing when you hear the sound.
mistakes.r: Start on seeing the flash (light arrives almost instantly) and stop on hearing the sound.

exam.q: State the equation that links wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: wave speed = frequency x wavelength
exam.tip: Words or symbols both score.

exam.q: A water wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 0.05 m. Calculate its speed.
exam.tip: Write the equation first.

exam.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s and has a frequency of 680 Hz. Calculate its wavelength.
model: lambda = v / f
exam.tip: Rearrangement mark comes first.

exam.q: A radio wave has a wavelength of 1500 m. The speed of radio waves is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the frequency in kHz.
model: = 200 kHz
exam.tip: Watch the unit asked for.

exam.q: Explain why a student measures the length of ten waves in a ripple tank rather than one.
model: A single wavelength is small so the uncertainty in measuring it is large compared with its size.
Measuring ten and dividing by ten reduces the (percentage) uncertainty.
exam.tip: Use the word uncertainty.

exam.q: A student stands 85 m from a wall and claps. The echo is heard 0.50 s later. Calculate the speed of sound.
model: distance = 2 x 85 = 170 m
exam.tip: Double the distance.

exam.q: The frequency of the dipper in a ripple tank is doubled. The depth of water is unchanged. State and explain what happens to the wavelength.
model: Wave speed stays the same because the medium/depth is unchanged.
v = f x lambda, so if f doubles
wavelength halves.
exam.tip: Say what stays constant and why.

exam.q: Two microphones are placed 1.5 m apart. A timer records that a clap took 4.4 ms to travel from one to the other. Calculate the speed of sound and suggest why this method is better than using a stopwatch.
model: Electronic timing has no human reaction time
so the time measured is more accurate/precise.
exam.tip: Convert ms to s.

exam.q: Describe how to use a ripple tank to determine the speed of water waves. Include the measurements you would take and how you would use them.
model: Set up the ripple tank with water of constant depth, level tank, lamp above and white paper below.
Switch on the motor so the dipper/bar makes waves of constant frequency.
Measure frequency by counting waves passing a point in a measured time (e.g. 10 s) and dividing, or read from the supply / stroboscope.
Place a ruler on the paper, photograph the pattern, and measure the length of several (e.g. 10) wavelengths; divide to find one wavelength.
Calculate speed using wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
Repeat and take a mean; alternatively time one wave across a measured length of tank and use speed = distance / time as a check.
exam.tip: Structure: set-up, frequency, wavelength, calculation, improve accuracy.

exam.q: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air outdoors, and explain how to make the result as accurate as possible.
model: Measure a large distance (e.g. 100 m+) using a trundle wheel / tape measure.
One person makes a loud sound with a visible action, e.g. cymbals or starting pistol (or clap facing a wall for echo).
The other starts a stopwatch on seeing the action and stops on hearing the sound (or times echo intervals).
speed = distance / time (using 2d for echoes).
Use a large distance so the time is large compared with reaction time.
Repeat several times, swap positions to cancel wind, and calculate a mean.
exam.tip: Every improvement should be linked to the error it reduces.

worked.q: In a ripple tank, 12 waves pass a point in 6.0 s. A photo shows that 8 wavelengths occupy 24 cm. Calculate the wave speed.
steps: Frequency = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 Hz.
Wavelength = 24 cm / 8 = 3.0 cm = 0.030 m.
v = f x lambda = 2.0 x 0.030.

worked.q: A student times 20 echo intervals as 12.0 s, standing 100 m from a wall. Find the speed of sound.
steps: Time for one echo round trip = 12.0 / 20 = 0.60 s.
Distance for one round trip = 2 x 100 = 200 m.
Speed = distance / time = 200 / 0.60.
Speed = 333 m/s (3 s.f.).
worked.ans: about 330 m/s

worked.q: A mobile phone signal has a frequency of 1.8 GHz. Electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the wavelength.
steps: Convert: 1.8 GHz = 1.8 x 10^9 Hz.
lambda = 0.167 m.
worked.ans: 0.17 m (about 17 cm)

phy_ocrb.0.6.summary: When a wave meets a **boundary (interface) between two media** it can be **reflected**, **transmitted** or absorbed; transmitted waves may be **refracted**. Reflection obeys the law **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**. Refraction is the change of direction that happens because the **wave speed changes** as the wave enters a new medium: the frequency stays the same, so the **wavelength changes**, and wavefronts arriving at an angle bend towards the normal when they slow down and away from it when they speed up. PAG8 investigates this with a ray box and glass or perspex blocks.

core.p: An **interface** (boundary) is where two different media meet, such as air and glass, or deep and shallow water. When a wave reaches one, some or all of it can be **reflected** back, **transmitted** into the new medium, or **absorbed** by it.
bullets: Reflection: the wave bounces back into the first medium.
Transmission: the wave passes through into the second medium.
Absorption: the wave's energy is transferred to the material (e.g. heating it).
Usually a mixture happens: e.g. light hitting a window is mostly transmitted but some is reflected (you see a faint reflection).
Refraction is a change of direction of a transmitted wave caused by a change of speed.

core.p: All angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the **normal**, an imaginary line drawn **at 90 degrees to the surface** at the point where the ray hits. Measuring from the normal works even for curved surfaces.
bullets: Angle of incidence (i): between the incident ray and the normal.
Angle of reflection (r): between the reflected ray and the normal.
Angle of refraction: between the refracted ray and the normal.
Draw the normal as a dashed line with a ruler.
Never measure from the surface itself.

callouts.p: A line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray meets it.
An angle measured from the surface gives 90 minus the correct angle.

core.h: Reflection and the law of reflection
core.p: When a wave reflects from a smooth flat surface, it leaves at the same angle it arrived. This is the **law of reflection**. The wave speed, frequency and wavelength do not change because the wave stays in the same medium.
bullets: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**.
Incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.
Smooth surfaces give **specular** reflection: a clear image, as in a mirror.
Rough surfaces give **diffuse** reflection: each part of the surface has a different normal, so rays scatter in many directions and no clear image forms (the law still holds for each ray).
Water waves in a ripple tank reflect off a barrier obeying the same law; sound reflects to give echoes.

callouts.p: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

fig.cap: Reflection at a plane mirror. The angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r; both are measured from the normal, drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror.

core.p: Refraction is the **change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary at an angle**, caused by a change in speed. Light entering glass from air slows down and **bends towards the normal**; light leaving glass into air speeds up and **bends away from the normal**.
bullets: Entering a medium where it travels **slower** (e.g. air to glass, air to water): bends **towards** the normal; angle of refraction is smaller than angle of incidence.
Entering a medium where it travels **faster** (glass to air): bends **away** from the normal.
Along the normal (angle of incidence 0 degrees): **no change in direction**, but the speed and wavelength still change.
In a rectangular block, the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
Some light is always reflected at each surface too.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, because its speed changes.

core.h: Why the speed changes but the frequency does not
core.p: The **frequency is set by the source** and cannot change at a boundary: every wave that arrives at the boundary per second must leave it per second, otherwise waves would pile up or vanish. The **speed depends on the medium**. So from v = f x lambda, if v falls and f is fixed, **lambda must fall in the same proportion**.
bullets: Light travels slower in glass (about 2 x 10^8 m/s) than in air (about 3 x 10^8 m/s).
Water waves travel slower in **shallow** water than in deep water.
Sound travels faster in water and solids than in air, so sound bends away from the normal entering water from air.
Wavelength shorter in the slower medium: wavefronts are closer together.
Frequency, and so colour of light, is unchanged by refraction.

callouts.p: At a boundary: frequency stays the same; speed changes; therefore wavelength changes.

core.p: A **wavefront** is a line joining points on the same crest. When a wavefront hits a boundary **at an angle**, one end enters the slower medium first and slows down while the other end is still moving fast in the first medium. The part still in the fast medium travels further in the same time, so the **wavefront swings round and changes direction**.
bullets: Step 1: wavefront arrives at an angle, so one side reaches the boundary first.
Step 2: that side slows down in the new medium.
Step 3: the other side is still travelling at the higher speed, so it covers more distance in the same time.
Step 4: the wavefront pivots, so the direction of travel bends towards the normal.
Step 5: wavefronts in the slow medium are closer together (shorter wavelength) because frequency is unchanged.
If the wavefront arrives parallel to the boundary (along the normal), the whole front slows at once, so it does not turn.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: 'one part of the wavefront slows down first', 'the rest is still faster', 'so the wave changes direction'.

core.h: Refraction of water waves in a ripple tank
core.p: A ripple tank shows refraction clearly. A sheet of glass or perspex placed in the tank makes a region of **shallow water**. Waves crossing into it slow down and their wavelength shortens.
bullets: Place the perspex at an angle to the wavefronts to see them change direction.
Place it parallel to the wavefronts to see only a wavelength change.
The frequency of the dipper is the same for both regions.
Coastlines: waves slow in shallow water near beaches, so wavefronts bend to become nearly parallel to the shore.

core.h: PAG8: investigating refraction with a ray box
core.p: In PAG8 you shine a narrow ray of light from a **ray box** (with a slit) into a rectangular **glass or perspex block** and measure how much it bends for different angles of incidence.
bullets: Place the block on white paper and draw round it with a sharp pencil.
Draw a **normal** at 90 degrees to one long side using a protractor.
Shine the ray at the point where the normal meets the block, at a measured angle of incidence (e.g. 10, 20, ... 70 degrees).
Mark the emergent ray with two crosses far apart; remove the block and join the entry and exit points to show the refracted ray.
Measure the angle of refraction from the normal with a protractor.
Repeat for each angle; plot angle of refraction against angle of incidence.
The same set-up with a plane mirror on a line lets you check the law of reflection.

head: Variable
In PAG8 refraction
rows: same block material, same ray box, same wavelength (colour) of light

callouts.p: Dark room and a narrow ray are needed for precise angles; a wide ray makes the angle uncertain.

core.p: Small errors in drawing lines lead to large errors in angles, so method matters.
bullets: Use a **thin ray** (narrow slit) and mark its centre.
Place crosses **far apart** along each ray to draw lines more accurately.
Read the protractor at eye level to avoid parallax.
Repeat each angle and calculate a mean.
Results: angle of refraction is always smaller than angle of incidence for air into glass, and the difference grows as i increases.
Safety: ray box lamps get hot; do not touch the bulb; take care with glass block edges.

core.p: Different materials slow light by different amounts. The more a material slows the light, the **more** the light bends at the boundary for the same angle of incidence.
bullets: Glass bends light more than water because light travels slower in glass than in water.
To compare materials fairly, keep the angle of incidence the same.
If a material bends the light more, light travels more slowly in it.
Sound bends the opposite way to light at an air-water boundary because sound speeds up in water.

core.h: Linking reflection, refraction and wave speed
core.p: Reflection keeps the wave in the same medium, so speed, frequency and wavelength are all unchanged. Refraction moves it into a new medium, so speed and wavelength change while frequency is constant.
bullets: Reflection: same medium, same speed, same wavelength, angle i = angle r.
Refraction: new medium, new speed, new wavelength, same frequency, new direction (unless along the normal).
Both are described using the normal.
Both happen together at most real boundaries.

analogy.t: A line of marching soldiers walking from a road onto mud
analogy.p: Picture soldiers marching side by side in a row (a wavefront) who cross from a smooth road onto thick mud at an angle. The soldiers who reach the mud first slow down while those still on the road keep their pace, so the row swings round and the whole line changes direction, bending towards the normal. Their step rate (frequency) stays the same, but their steps get shorter in the mud (shorter wavelength). If they walked onto the mud head-on, everyone would slow together and the line would not turn. It breaks down because soldiers are real objects that travel across the boundary, while in a wave it is energy, not matter, that moves.

terms.d: The surface where two different media meet.
A material that a wave travels through, e.g. air, glass, water.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
A wave bouncing back from a boundary into the medium it came from.
The change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary at an angle, caused by a change in speed.
A wave passing through a material or boundary.
Energy of a wave being transferred to the material it hits.
A line joining neighbouring points on a wave that are in step, e.g. along one crest.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction, giving a clear image.
Reflection from a rough surface, scattering light in many directions.
A lamp in a box with a slit, producing a narrow ray of light for ray experiments.
The ray that leaves a block or lens after refraction.

mistakes.w: Angles measured from the surface of the mirror or block.
mistakes.r: Angles are measured from the normal.

mistakes.w: Refraction is when light bends.
mistakes.r: Refraction is the change in direction caused by a change in speed as a wave enters a different medium.

mistakes.w: The frequency changes when light enters glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.w: Light speeds up in glass so it bends towards the normal.
mistakes.r: Light slows down in glass and bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: A ray entering along the normal is not refracted, so nothing changes.
mistakes.r: Direction does not change, but speed and wavelength still change.

mistakes.w: Light bends because the glass is denser, with no mention of speed.
mistakes.r: Explain using change in wave speed: one side of the wavefront slows first, so the wave changes direction.

exam.q: State the law of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
exam.tip: Mention the normal for full security.

exam.q: What is meant by the normal in a ray diagram?
model: A line at 90 degrees to the surface where the ray meets it.
exam.tip: Say 'at right angles to the surface'.

exam.q: Light travels from air into glass. State what happens to its speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: Speed decreases.
Frequency stays the same.
Wavelength decreases.
exam.tip: Three separate statements, one per mark.

exam.q: A ray of light hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35 degrees. State the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror surface.
model: Angle of reflection = 35 degrees from the normal
Angle to surface = 90 - 35 = 55 degrees
exam.tip: Read carefully: from the surface, not the normal.

exam.q: Explain why a ray of light entering a glass block along the normal does not change direction.
model: The whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same time.
So all of it slows down together and no part gets ahead, so no change in direction (speed still decreases).
exam.tip: Use wavefront ideas.

exam.q: Water waves move from deep to shallow water. The frequency is 5 Hz. In deep water the wavelength is 4 cm; in shallow water it is 2.5 cm. Calculate the change in wave speed.
model: Shallow: v = 5 x 0.025 = 0.125 m/s
Decrease of 0.075 m/s
exam.tip: Frequency is the same in both.

exam.q: Explain, using ideas about wave speed and wavefronts, why light changes direction when it passes from air into glass at an angle.
model: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
The wavefront meets the boundary at an angle, so one side enters the glass first and slows down first.
The other side is still in air moving faster, so travels further in the same time.
The wavefront turns / changes direction, bending towards the normal (and wavelength shortens).
exam.tip: Speed change plus 'one part before the other' is essential.

exam.q: Sound travels faster in water than in air. A sound wave passes from air into water at an angle. Predict the direction it bends and explain.
model: It bends away from the normal.
Because it speeds up in water.
The part of the wavefront entering the water first speeds up and gets ahead, turning the wavefront.
exam.tip: Opposite of light: check which medium is faster.

exam.q: A student finds the angles of refraction for light entering a perspex block are always smaller than the angles of incidence. Explain what this shows.
model: Light bends towards the normal on entering the perspex.
So light travels more slowly in perspex than in air.
exam.tip: Link the bending direction to the speed change.

exam.q: Describe how to carry out an experiment (PAG8) to investigate how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence for light entering a glass block. Include how to make the results accurate.
model: Place the glass block on white paper and draw round it; draw a normal at 90 degrees to one side with a protractor.
Use a ray box with a narrow slit to shine a ray at the point where the normal meets the block, at a measured angle of incidence.
Mark the emerging ray with crosses far apart, remove the block and join the entry and exit points to draw the refracted ray.
Measure the angle of refraction from the normal with a protractor.
Repeat for a range of angles (e.g. 10 to 70 degrees in 10 degree steps) and repeat each to find a mean.
Accuracy: dim room, thin ray, sharp pencil, crosses far apart, read protractor at eye level; plot a graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence.
exam.tip: A logical sequence earns the top band: set-up, measurement, range, repeats, analysis.

worked.q: Light of frequency 5.0 x 10^14 Hz travels from air (speed 3.0 x 10^8 m/s) into glass (speed 2.0 x 10^8 m/s). Calculate its wavelength in air and in glass.
steps: Frequency is unchanged at the boundary: f = 5.0 x 10^14 Hz in both.
Check: speed fell by a factor of 1.5, wavelength fell by the same factor.
worked.ans: 6.0 x 10^-7 m in air; 4.0 x 10^-7 m in glass.

worked.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 25 degrees to the mirror surface. Find the angle of incidence, angle of reflection and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
steps: Angle to normal = 90 - 25 = 65 degrees, so angle of incidence = 65 degrees.
Law of reflection: angle of reflection = 65 degrees.
Angle between rays = 65 + 65 = 130 degrees.
worked.ans: i = 65 degrees, r = 65 degrees, angle between rays = 130 degrees.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a ray leaving a rectangular glass block is parallel to the ray that entered it.
steps: On entering, the light slows down and bends towards the normal.
On leaving, it speeds up by the same amount (back to its speed in air) and bends away from the normal.
The two faces are parallel so the normals are parallel, and the changes in direction are equal and opposite.
So the emergent ray travels in the same direction as the incident ray, but displaced sideways.
worked.ans: Equal and opposite changes of speed at parallel faces give equal and opposite bending, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.

phy_ocrb.0.7.summary: Ray diagrams model light as straight lines (rays) with arrows to predict where light goes and where images form. For **reflection** the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; for **refraction** the ray bends towards the normal on slowing down and away on speeding up; in **dispersion** a prism splits white light into a spectrum because each colour (frequency) slows by a different amount, so violet is refracted most and red least. A **convex (converging) lens** brings parallel rays together at the **principal focus** and can form real or virtual images depending on where the object is, while a **concave (diverging) lens** spreads parallel rays out as if from a virtual principal focus and always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.

core.p: A ray diagram is a precise drawing, and marks are lost for sloppy construction. Rays are straight lines showing the direction light travels.
bullets: Use a **sharp pencil and a ruler** for every ray.
Put an **arrow on each ray** to show the direction of travel.
Draw the **normal** as a dashed line at 90 degrees to the surface at the point where a ray meets it.
Measure angles from the normal with a protractor.
Real rays are solid lines; **virtual rays** (where light only appears to come from) are dashed.
Label the object, image, focal points (F) and any angles.

callouts.p: Missing arrows or freehand rays commonly cost a mark even if the geometry is right.

core.p: For a plane mirror, every ray obeys **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, measured from the normal. To draw: mark the point where the ray hits, draw the normal, measure the incident angle, then draw the reflected ray at the same angle on the other side of the normal.
bullets: Incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in the same plane.
Smooth surfaces give specular reflection; rough surfaces give diffuse reflection (normals point in different directions).
A ray hitting a mirror along the normal reflects straight back.
Two mirrors at 90 degrees send a ray back parallel to its original path (used in bike reflectors).

core.h: The image in a plane mirror
core.p: Rays from an object reflect off a mirror and enter the eye. The brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays back behind the mirror to where they appear to come from. That point is the **virtual image**.
bullets: The image is **virtual**: no light actually passes through it, so it cannot be shown on a screen.
It is **upright** (the same way up as the object).
It is the **same size** as the object.
It is the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front.
It is **laterally inverted** (left and right swapped).
To construct: draw two rays from the object, reflect each using i = r, extend the reflected rays backwards as dashed lines; where they meet is the image.

callouts.p: An image formed where rays only appear to come from; it cannot be projected onto a screen.

core.p: At each boundary draw the normal, then decide whether the light is slowing down (bend towards the normal) or speeding up (bend away). For a rectangular block the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
bullets: Air to glass or water: slows, **bends towards the normal**; angle of refraction smaller than angle of incidence.
Glass or water to air: speeds up, **bends away from the normal**.
Along the normal: no change in direction.
Through a rectangular block: ray displaced sideways but leaves parallel to how it entered.
Through a triangular prism: both surfaces bend the ray towards the thicker base, so it is deviated overall.

callouts.p: Do not let the ray bend at the normal line itself; it bends only at the boundary surface.

core.p: White light is a mixture of colours, each with a different frequency. In glass, **different frequencies travel at slightly different speeds**: violet light slows the most, red the least. So at each face of a prism **violet is refracted (bent) most and red least**, and the colours spread out into a **spectrum**. This splitting is called **dispersion**.
bullets: Order of the visible spectrum: **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet** (red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency).
Red is deviated least; violet is deviated most (towards the base of the prism).
A triangular prism shows dispersion clearly because the two faces are not parallel, so the spreading adds up rather than cancelling as in a rectangular block.
Rainbows are dispersion by water droplets.
On a ray diagram, show one white ray entering and a fan of coloured rays leaving, labelled red at the top (least bent) and violet at the bottom.

callouts.p: The splitting of white light into a spectrum of colours because each colour is refracted by a different amount.
Different colours travel at different speeds in glass, so they are refracted by different amounts.

core.p: A lens refracts light at both of its curved surfaces to change the direction of rays in a controlled way. Its shape decides whether it brings rays together or spreads them apart.
bullets: **Convex (converging) lens**: thicker in the middle; makes parallel rays converge to a point.
**Concave (diverging) lens**: thinner in the middle; makes parallel rays spread out (diverge).
Ray diagrams often draw lenses as a vertical line with outward arrows (convex) or inward-pointing arrows / V ends (concave) on the symbol.
In ray diagrams, all the bending is drawn as happening once, at the centre line of the lens.
The **principal axis** is the line through the centre of the lens at 90 degrees to it.

head: Feature
Convex lens
Concave lens
rows: diverge as if from principal focus
magnifying glass, camera, projector, correcting long sight

core.p: Rays travelling **parallel to the principal axis** are bent by a convex lens so they all pass through one point: the **principal focus (F)**. The distance from the centre of the lens to F is the **focal length (f)**. There is a principal focus on each side of a lens, at the same distance.
bullets: Convex lens: parallel rays actually meet at F, so it is a **real** focus.
Concave lens: parallel rays spread out as if they came from F on the same side as the incoming light; this is a **virtual** focus, drawn with dashed lines.
A **more curved (fatter) lens** refracts light more and has a **shorter focal length**, so it is more powerful.
You can estimate f of a convex lens by focusing a distant object (e.g. a window) onto a screen and measuring the lens-to-screen distance.

callouts.p: The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after passing through a convex lens (or appear to come from, for a concave lens).
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

core.h: The three construction rays for a convex lens
core.p: To find an image you only need two rays from the top of the object; a third checks your drawing. Where the rays cross after the lens is the top of the image.
bullets: **Ray 1:** parallel to the principal axis, then refracted **through F** on the far side.
**Ray 2:** straight **through the centre** of the lens, undeviated.
**Ray 3:** through F on the near side, then emerges **parallel** to the principal axis.
Draw the image as an arrow from the principal axis to where the rays cross.
If rays diverge after the lens, extend them backwards as dashed lines; where they meet is a virtual image.

callouts.p: Rays 1 and 2 are the easiest to draw accurately; use ray 3 only as a check.

core.h: Images formed by a convex lens
core.p: The type of image depends on how far the object is from the lens compared with the focal length. Describe any image with three words: **real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished**.
bullets: Real images form where rays actually meet, on the opposite side to the object, and can be projected onto a screen; they are always inverted for a single lens.
Virtual images form where rays only appear to come from, on the same side as the object; they are upright.
As the object moves closer to F, the real image moves further away and gets bigger.
Object exactly at F: rays leave parallel, so no image forms.

head: Object position
Image
Use
rows: real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F
virtual, upright, magnified, same side as object

callouts.p: An image formed where rays of light actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen.

core.h: Convex lens as a magnifying glass
core.p: When the object is **closer to the lens than F**, the rays leaving the lens diverge and never meet. The eye traces them back to a point behind the object, seeing a **virtual, upright, magnified** image.
bullets: Draw ray 1 (parallel then through F) and ray 2 (through centre).
Both diverge after the lens; extend both backwards with dashed lines.
They meet on the same side as the object, further away and higher up: the virtual image.
This is how a magnifying glass works.

core.h: Images formed by a concave lens
core.p: A concave lens always spreads light out, so rays from an object never meet after the lens. The image is always **virtual, upright and diminished**, on the same side of the lens as the object and between F and the lens.
bullets: Ray 1: parallel to the axis, then diverges as if from F on the object side (draw the dashed line back to F).
Ray 2: straight through the centre of the lens, undeviated.
Where ray 2 and the dashed backward extension of ray 1 meet is the top of the virtual image.
The image type does not depend on object distance.
Used in spectacles to correct short sight.

callouts.p: Concave lens: always virtual, upright, diminished.

core.h: Why lenses bend light: linking to wave speed
core.p: Lenses work by refraction: light slows down in glass. Because the lens surfaces are curved, the normal points in a different direction at each place on the surface, so rays at different heights are bent by different amounts.
bullets: Convex lens: rays further from the axis hit a more steeply sloping surface and are bent more, so all parallel rays meet at F.
Concave lens: the surfaces slope the other way, so rays are bent away from the axis.
Wave model: in a convex lens the middle of a wavefront travels through the thickest glass, so is slowed most, making the wavefront curve inwards and converge.
Different colours have slightly different focal lengths (dispersion again), which can give coloured fringes.

analogy.t: A convex lens is like a crowd funnelling to a stadium gate
analogy.p: Picture lots of people walking in parallel lines across a field towards a stadium. Stewards at a curved fence (the lens) redirect each line: people at the edges are turned most sharply and those in the middle walk straight on, so all lines meet at the gate (the principal focus). A concave lens is like stewards sending people outward to spread across a car park; if you look back from the car park, everyone seems to have come from one spot behind the fence (the virtual focus). It breaks down because light is not steered by anyone: it bends because its speed changes in glass, and people do not split into colours the way white light does.

terms.d: A straight line with an arrow showing the direction in which light travels.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
The change in direction of light at a boundary because its speed changes.
The splitting of white light into its colours because each colour is refracted by a different amount.
The band of colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet produced by dispersion.
A triangular block of glass or perspex used to refract and disperse light.
A lens thicker in the middle that makes parallel rays converge to a point.
A lens thinner in the middle that makes parallel rays spread out.
The line through the centre of a lens at right angles to the lens.
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (convex) or appear to come from (concave) after passing through a lens.
The distance from the centre of a lens to its principal focus.
An image formed where rays actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen.
An image formed where rays only appear to come from; it cannot be projected onto a screen.
Larger than / smaller than the object.
Reversed left to right, as an image in a plane mirror.

mistakes.w: Rays drawn without arrows or freehand.
mistakes.r: Use a ruler and put an arrow on every ray to show direction.

mistakes.w: Red light is bent the most by a prism.
mistakes.r: Violet is refracted most (slowed most); red is refracted least.

mistakes.w: A prism adds colour to white light.
mistakes.r: White light is already a mixture of colours; the prism separates them (dispersion).

mistakes.w: A ray through the centre of a convex lens goes through F.
mistakes.r: A ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.

mistakes.w: The image in a plane mirror is on the surface of the mirror / is real.
mistakes.r: It is virtual, the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

mistakes.w: A concave lens can form a real image.
mistakes.r: A concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.

mistakes.w: Focal length is the distance from the object to the lens.
mistakes.r: Focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

mistakes.w: A thicker lens has a longer focal length.
mistakes.r: A more curved (thicker) lens refracts more strongly and has a shorter focal length.

mistakes.w: Virtual rays drawn as solid lines.
mistakes.r: Rays that light only appears to follow are drawn dashed.

exam.q: What is meant by the focal length of a lens?
model: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
exam.tip: Say 'centre of the lens'.

exam.q: State two differences between a real image and a virtual image.
model: Real: rays actually meet; virtual: rays only appear to come from it.
Real can be projected on a screen; virtual cannot.
exam.tip: Compare both types in each point.

exam.q: Name the type of lens used as a magnifying glass and describe the image it forms.
model: Convex (converging) lens.
Virtual, upright, magnified.
exam.tip: Three-word descriptions are expected.

exam.q: Describe what happens to rays of light parallel to the principal axis when they pass through (a) a convex lens and (b) a concave lens.
model: (a) They converge / are brought together at the principal focus.
(b) They diverge / spread out as if from the principal focus on the near side.
exam.tip: Use converge and diverge.

exam.q: White light enters a glass prism and a spectrum is produced. Explain why.
model: White light is a mixture of colours/frequencies.
Each colour travels at a different speed in glass.
So each is refracted by a different amount (violet most, red least), spreading them out.
exam.tip: Link speed to amount of refraction.

exam.q: Draw a ray diagram to show how a plane mirror forms an image of a point object, and state where the image is.
model: Two rays from the object reflected with angle i = angle r (normals drawn).
Reflected rays extended back behind the mirror as dashed lines.
Image where dashed lines meet, same distance behind the mirror as object is in front.
exam.tip: Arrows and dashed virtual rays.

exam.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Describe the image formed.
model: Object is beyond 2F (20 cm).
Image is real and inverted.
Diminished, formed between F and 2F on the other side.
exam.tip: Compare the object distance with f and 2f first.

exam.q: An object is placed 6 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Explain, with reference to rays, why the image is virtual.
model: Object is between F and the lens.
Rays leaving the lens diverge and never meet.
They only appear to come from a point on the same side as the object, so the image is virtual (upright, magnified).
exam.tip: Explain in terms of rays, not just positions.

exam.q: Describe how to construct a ray diagram to find the image formed by a convex lens of an object placed between F and 2F, and state the nature of the image.
model: Ray from top of object parallel to axis, refracted through F on far side.
Ray from top of object straight through centre of lens, undeviated.
Where the rays cross is the top of the image; draw image down to the axis.
Image is real, inverted, magnified, beyond 2F.
exam.tip: Name each ray rule precisely.

exam.q: Compare how convex and concave lenses affect light and the images they form. Use ray diagram ideas in your answer.
model: Convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays to a real principal focus.
Concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges parallel rays as if from a virtual principal focus (dashed lines back).
Both bend light by refraction because light slows in glass; ray through centre is undeviated for both.
Convex lens forms real, inverted images when object is beyond F (size depends on distance relative to 2F).
Convex lens forms virtual, upright, magnified image when object is inside F (magnifying glass).
Concave lens always forms virtual, upright, diminished image on the same side as the object.
exam.tip: Cover effect on rays, focus type, image types and uses.

worked.q: Construct the image of a 2 cm tall object placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 5 cm (scale 1 square = 1 cm). Describe the image.
steps: Draw principal axis and lens; mark F at 5 cm and 2F at 10 cm each side.
Object arrow at 15 cm (beyond 2F), 2 cm tall.
Ray 1: from top, parallel to axis to lens, then through F on the far side.
Ray 2: from top, straight through lens centre.
Rays cross at about 7.5 cm beyond the lens, 1 cm below the axis.
Image lies between F and 2F.
worked.ans: Real, inverted, diminished (about 1 cm tall), about 7.5 cm from the lens on the opposite side.

worked.q: A beam of white light passes into a prism. Light of which colour leaves the prism closest to the base, and why?
steps: Dispersion: different colours travel at different speeds in glass.
Violet (highest frequency, shortest wavelength) slows down most.
Greatest change of speed means greatest change of direction at each face.
So violet is deviated most, towards the base.
worked.ans: Violet, because it is slowed and refracted the most.

worked.q: Model answer: why is the image in a plane mirror described as virtual?
steps: Light from the object reflects off the front of the mirror; no light passes behind it.
The reflected rays diverge into the eye.
The brain assumes light travels in straight lines and traces the rays back to a point behind the mirror.
No rays actually meet there, so the image cannot be shown on a screen.
worked.ans: Because the rays only appear to come from the image point behind the mirror; they do not actually meet there.

phy_ocrb.0.8.summary: When light (or any wave) meets the boundary between two materials it can be **reflected**, **transmitted** (often with refraction), **absorbed** or **scattered**, and usually a mixture of these happens at once. The colour we see an object as depends on which wavelengths of visible light it **reflects or transmits** and which it **absorbs**. Coloured filters work by transmitting only some wavelengths and absorbing the rest, so you can predict the colour of any object under any coloured light by tracking which wavelengths survive to reach the eye.

core.h: Four things that can happen at an interface
core.p: An **interface** (boundary) is where one material meets another, such as air and glass. When a wave arrives at an interface, its energy is shared out between several outcomes. Which outcome dominates depends on the two materials, the wavelength of the wave and the nature of the surface.
bullets: **Reflection**: the wave bounces back into the first material.
**Transmission**: the wave passes through into the second material and carries on; if it hits at an angle it usually changes direction (**refraction**).
**Absorption**: the energy of the wave is transferred to the material, usually warming it (energy goes to its thermal store).
**Scattering**: the wave is sent off in many different directions, for example by a rough surface or by small particles.
In reality a mixture usually happens: a window transmits most light but also reflects a little (you can see your reflection at night) and absorbs a little.
The total energy is conserved: energy reflected + energy transmitted + energy absorbed = energy arriving.

callouts.p: Exam answers often need you to say that **some** of the wave is reflected, **some** transmitted and **some** absorbed. Do not assume it is all-or-nothing.

core.p: How much light a material transmits decides how it looks. Materials are described by how they let light through.
bullets: **Transparent** materials (clear glass, water, clear plastic) transmit light with very little scattering, so you can see clearly through them.
**Translucent** materials (frosted glass, tracing paper, thin fabric) transmit light but scatter it, so you cannot see a clear image through them.
**Opaque** materials (wood, metal, brick) transmit no light; the light is either absorbed or reflected at the surface.
A material can be transparent to one wavelength and opaque to another: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet; your body is opaque to visible light but transmits X-rays.
Coloured transparent materials (stained glass, a red filter) transmit some colours and absorb the others.

core.p: Reflection always obeys the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal) for each individual ray. What differs between surfaces is whether the normals all point the same way.
bullets: **Specular reflection** happens at a **smooth** surface such as a mirror or still water: parallel rays stay parallel after reflection, so a clear image forms.
**Diffuse reflection** happens at a **rough** surface such as paper or a painted wall: each tiny part of the surface faces a different way, so parallel rays are **scattered** in many directions.
Diffuse reflection is why you can see an object from any angle, and why paper does not act as a mirror.
Each ray in diffuse reflection still obeys the law of reflection; only the normals differ.
Whether a surface counts as smooth depends on the wavelength: bumps much smaller than the wavelength do not scatter it.

callouts.t: Diffuse does not break the law
callouts.p: Students often write that the law of reflection is not obeyed in diffuse reflection. It is obeyed for every ray; the surface normals point in different directions.

core.h: White light is a mixture of colours
core.p: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Each colour corresponds to a different range of wavelengths (and frequencies).
bullets: White light is a mixture of all visible wavelengths, from **red** (longest wavelength, about 700 nm, lowest frequency) to **violet** (shortest wavelength, about 400 nm, highest frequency).
The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
A prism can split white light into these colours (dispersion), showing white really is a mixture.
Our eyes detect colour using cells sensitive to different ranges of wavelength; the brain interprets the mixture arriving as a colour.
If no visible light reaches the eye from an object, we see it as **black**.

callouts.p: A **different colour** means a **different wavelength** (and frequency) of visible light.

core.p: The colour of an opaque object depends on **differential absorption and reflection**: the object absorbs some wavelengths and reflects others. The colour we see is the colour of the light that is **reflected** into our eyes.
bullets: A red apple in white light **reflects red** light and **absorbs** all the other colours, so it looks red.
A white object **reflects all** visible wavelengths (roughly equally), so it looks white.
A black object **absorbs all** visible wavelengths and reflects none, so it looks black.
A green leaf reflects mainly green and absorbs red and blue (which the plant uses for photosynthesis).
The absorbed energy warms the object, which is why black objects get hotter in sunlight than white ones.
The reflected light is usually diffusely reflected, which is why the colour is visible from many directions.

callouts.p: An opaque object appears the colour of the wavelengths of light it **reflects**; all other wavelengths are **absorbed**.

fig.cap: A red object in white light: red wavelengths are reflected to the eye, all other wavelengths are absorbed, so the object appears red.

core.h: Why transparent coloured objects have colour
core.p: For a transparent or translucent coloured object, the colour seen is the colour of the light it **transmits**. This is **differential absorption and transmission**.
bullets: Blue stained glass transmits blue light and absorbs the other colours, so light coming through it looks blue.
Clear (colourless) glass transmits all visible wavelengths roughly equally.
The deeper or thicker the coloured material, the more strongly the other colours are absorbed.

core.p: A **colour filter** is a transparent coloured material that **transmits** only a certain range of wavelengths and **absorbs** the rest. A filter cannot add colour to light; it can only remove wavelengths.
bullets: A **red filter** transmits red light and absorbs all other colours.
Shining white light through a red filter gives red light, which is dimmer than the original white light because energy has been absorbed.
Shining green light at a red filter: the green is absorbed and nothing gets through, so it looks dark (black).
Two filters in a row: only wavelengths transmitted by **both** get through. Red then green gives nothing (darkness).
Filters are used in stage lighting, photography and traffic lights (a white lamp behind a red, amber or green filter).

callouts.p: A red filter does not turn light red. It **removes** (absorbs) every colour except red. If the light had no red in it, nothing gets through.
