core.p: To predict an object's colour under coloured light, ask which wavelengths **arrive** and which of those the object **reflects**. Only light that is both present and reflected can reach your eye.
bullets: Red object in red light: red is present and reflected, so it looks **red**.
Red object in blue light: blue is absorbed and there is no red to reflect, so it looks **black**.
White object in red light: white reflects every colour, but only red arrives, so it looks **red**.
Black object in any light: everything is absorbed, so it looks **black**.
Green object seen through a red filter in white light: the object reflects green, the filter absorbs green, so it looks **black**.

callouts.p: Step 1: which colours are in the light hitting it? Step 2: which of those does it reflect? Whatever is left is what you see; if nothing is left, it is black.

core.p: When light is absorbed, its energy is transferred to the material. This links colour to heating and to the rest of the EM spectrum topic.
bullets: Absorbed light energy usually increases the **thermal energy store** of the material, so its temperature rises.
Dark surfaces absorb more visible light than pale ones and so warm up faster in sunlight.
Pale or shiny surfaces reflect more and absorb less, so they stay cooler (for example white buildings in hot countries).
The amount absorbed depends on the wavelength and the material, which is exactly why objects have different colours.

core.p: Reflection, transmission and absorption happen for all waves, not just light. The same ideas explain echoes, ultrasound and why some materials block certain radiation.
bullets: Sound is reflected at hard surfaces (echoes) and absorbed by soft materials such as curtains and foam.
Ultrasound is partly reflected at each boundary between different tissues, which is used in scanning.
Microwaves are reflected by metal and absorbed by water, which is how a microwave oven heats food.
X-rays are transmitted through soft tissue but absorbed by bone, giving the contrast in an X-ray image.
Generally, the more different the two materials are, the more of the wave is reflected at the interface.

core.h: Linking it together for long answers
core.p: Six mark questions often ask you to explain what is seen in a situation with lights, filters and coloured objects. Build the answer as a chain of cause and effect.
bullets: State what light is incident (which wavelengths).
State what happens at each surface or filter: which wavelengths are reflected, transmitted or absorbed.
State which wavelengths finally reach the eye.
Conclude with the colour seen, or black if none reach the eye.
Use the words **reflect**, **absorb**, **transmit** and **wavelength** precisely; avoid vague words like 'blocks' or 'lets in'.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward phrases like 'only red wavelengths are reflected' or 'green light is absorbed by the red filter'.

analogy.t: A colour bouncer at a club door
analogy.p: Think of an object or filter as a bouncer and each colour of light as a guest. A red filter is a bouncer who lets only red guests through and turns everyone else away (absorbs them). A red apple is a bouncer who sends red guests back out to you (reflects) and keeps the rest inside. If no red guests arrive at all, no one comes out, and the door looks dark. Where it breaks down: real objects do not perfectly sort colours; they reflect or transmit a spread of wavelengths in different amounts, and absorbed light does not wait inside but becomes thermal energy.

terms.d: The boundary between two different materials, where waves can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed.
When a wave bounces back from a surface into the material it came from.
When a wave passes through a material and continues on.
When the energy of a wave is transferred to the material it meets, usually heating it.
When a wave is sent off in many different directions by a rough surface or small particles.
Reflection from a smooth surface in which parallel incident rays remain parallel after reflection.
Reflection from a rough surface in which parallel incident rays are scattered in many directions.
A material that transmits light with little scattering, so clear images can be seen through it.
A material that transmits light but scatters it, so no clear image can be seen through it.
A material that does not transmit light; light is absorbed or reflected.
A mixture of all the wavelengths (colours) of visible light.
Absorbing some wavelengths of light more than others, which gives an object its colour.
A transparent material that transmits only certain wavelengths of light and absorbs the others.
A line drawn at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray hits it; angles are measured from it.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave; different visible wavelengths are seen as different colours.

mistakes.w: A red filter turns white light red / adds red colour.
mistakes.r: A red filter transmits red light and **absorbs** all other wavelengths; it removes colours, it does not add them.

mistakes.w: A red object absorbs red light.
mistakes.r: A red object **reflects** red light and **absorbs** the other colours.

mistakes.w: A black object reflects black light.
mistakes.r: There is no black light; a black object **absorbs all** visible wavelengths, so none reaches the eye.

mistakes.w: In diffuse reflection the law of reflection is not obeyed.
mistakes.r: Every ray obeys the law of reflection; the rough surface has normals in different directions so rays are scattered.

mistakes.w: A blue object looks red in red light.
mistakes.r: It looks **black**: red light is absorbed and there is no blue light to reflect.

mistakes.w: Translucent means you can see clearly through it.
mistakes.r: Translucent materials transmit light but **scatter** it so no clear image is seen; that clear description is transparent.

mistakes.w: Light either reflects or goes through, never both.
mistakes.r: At most interfaces some light is **reflected**, some **transmitted** and some **absorbed** at the same time.

mistakes.w: A white object in green light looks white.
mistakes.r: It looks **green**: it reflects all wavelengths, but only green is arriving.

exam.q: Name the type of reflection that happens at a plane mirror.
model: Specular reflection
exam.tip: Smooth surface = specular; rough surface = diffuse.

exam.q: Explain why a sheet of white paper does not form an image like a mirror does.
model: Paper is rough (on a small scale) so gives diffuse reflection
Parallel rays are scattered in different directions so no clear image forms
exam.tip: Mention both the rough surface and the scattering of rays.

exam.q: Explain why a ripe tomato looks red in daylight.
model: Daylight/white light contains all colours (wavelengths)
The tomato reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
exam.tip: Always say what is reflected AND what is absorbed.

exam.q: A student looks at a green T-shirt under red stage lighting. State and explain the colour the T-shirt appears.
model: Black
Red light is absorbed and there is no green light to reflect, so no light reaches the eye
exam.tip: Black is the colour seen when no light reaches the eye from the object.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a transparent and a translucent material.
model: Both transmit light
Transparent transmits with little scattering so a clear image is seen; translucent scatters the light so no clear image is seen
exam.tip: Scattering is the key word for translucent.

exam.q: White light is shone through a blue filter. Describe what happens to the light.
model: Blue light is transmitted
All other colours/wavelengths are absorbed (so the light is dimmer)
exam.tip: Use transmit and absorb, not 'lets through' and 'blocks'.

exam.q: Light is shone through a red filter and then a blue filter onto a white screen. State what is seen on the screen and explain why.
model: Screen appears dark/black (no light)
Red filter transmits only red light, absorbing the rest
Blue filter absorbs red light so no light reaches the screen
exam.tip: Track the light filter by filter.

exam.q: When light hits a glass window, describe three things that can happen to it.
model: Some is reflected
Most is transmitted (and refracted if at an angle)
Some is absorbed by the glass
exam.tip: A window does all three at once.

exam.q: Explain why black cars get hotter than white cars in sunlight.
model: Black surfaces absorb all/most visible wavelengths
White surfaces reflect most visible wavelengths
Absorbed energy is transferred to the thermal store of the car so its temperature rises more
exam.tip: Link absorption to energy transfer to the thermal store.

exam.q: A theatre designer has a white lamp, a red filter and a green filter, and actors wearing white, red and green costumes. Explain how the appearance of the costumes changes when the lamp is used with no filter, with the red filter and with the green filter.
model: White light contains all colours; costumes appear in their own colours
Coloured objects reflect their own colour and absorb other colours; white reflects all
Red filter transmits only red light and absorbs other colours
Under red light: white costume looks red, red looks red, green looks black
Green filter transmits only green light
Under green light: white looks green, green looks green, red looks black
exam.tip: Level 3 answers explain the reason (reflect/absorb/transmit) as well as stating each colour.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of wavelength, why different objects have different colours in white light.
model: White light is a mixture of wavelengths
Different colours correspond to different wavelengths
Objects absorb some wavelengths and reflect (or transmit) others
The colour seen is that of the wavelengths reflected or transmitted to the eye
exam.tip: Use the phrase differential absorption.

worked.q: A blue book with white writing is viewed in a room lit only by red light. Describe what the book looks like.
steps: Identify the incident light: only red wavelengths arrive.
Blue cover: reflects blue only, absorbs red. No blue arrives, so it reflects nothing and looks black.
White writing: reflects all wavelengths, so it reflects the red light and looks red.
Combine the two parts.
worked.ans: The book appears black with red writing.

worked.q: White light passes through a yellow filter (transmits red, yellow and green) and then a green filter. What colour light comes out?
steps: After the yellow filter: red, yellow and green transmitted; blue and violet absorbed.
The green filter transmits only green and absorbs red and yellow.
Only wavelengths transmitted by both filters survive: green.
worked.ans: Green light (dimmer than the original, because most energy has been absorbed).

worked.q: Explain why you can see a book from anywhere in a room, but can only see a reflection of a lamp in a mirror from certain positions.
steps: The book's surface is rough, giving diffuse reflection.
Light from each point is scattered in all directions, so some reaches your eye wherever you stand.
The mirror is smooth, giving specular reflection: each ray reflects at one angle only (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).
So reflected light from the lamp reaches your eye only if you are at the right angle.
worked.ans: Diffuse reflection scatters light from the book in all directions; specular reflection from the mirror sends light in one direction only.

phy_ocrb.0.9.summary: Sound is a **longitudinal** wave that can travel through solids, liquids and gases, and our ears work by turning vibrations in air into vibrations of solid parts (eardrum, small bones, cochlea), which only works well over a **limited frequency range** (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz for humans). **Ultrasound** (above 20 kHz) is partly reflected at boundaries between materials, and timing the **echoes** lets us find the depth of hidden structures, as in medical scans, flaw detection and **SONAR**. **Seismic waves** from earthquakes come as **P waves** (longitudinal) and **S waves** (transverse), and the way they travel through, or fail to travel through, the Earth gives evidence for its layered structure, including a **liquid outer core**.

core.p: Sound is a **mechanical, longitudinal** wave: particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.
bullets: Sound can travel through **solids**, liquids and gases.
In a solid the particles are close together and strongly linked, so vibrations are passed on quickly: sound is generally **fastest in solids**, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
Typical speeds: air about 340 m/s, water about 1500 m/s, steel about 5000 m/s or more.
When sound in air hits a solid surface, the pressure changes push the surface back and forth, making the solid **vibrate**; this is how sound passes into, and through, walls and windows.
The frequency of a wave does **not** change when it crosses into a new medium; the speed and wavelength change (v = f x wavelength).

callouts.p: When sound passes from air into a solid, its **speed and wavelength increase**, but its **frequency is unchanged** (it is set by the source).

core.p: The ear converts sound waves in air into vibrations of solid structures and then into electrical signals for the brain.
bullets: Sound waves travel down the **ear canal** to the **eardrum**.
The pressure variations make the eardrum (a thin membrane) **vibrate** at the same frequency as the sound.
These vibrations are passed through three **small bones** (ossicles) in the middle ear, which pass on the vibrations to the inner ear.
In the **cochlea** (inner ear), the vibrations move fluid and tiny hair cells, which produce electrical signals.
The **auditory nerve** carries the signals to the brain, which interprets them as sound.
Different parts of the cochlea respond to different frequencies.

callouts.t: Sound in air to vibration in solids
callouts.p: Hearing depends on converting **sound waves in air** into **vibrations in solids** (eardrum and small bones). This conversion works only over a **limited frequency range**.

core.h: The limited range of human hearing
core.p: Humans can hear frequencies from about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**. The limits exist because the eardrum, bones and cochlea can only vibrate effectively over a certain range of frequencies.
bullets: Below about 20 Hz is **infrasound**; above about 20 kHz is **ultrasound**. Neither can be heard by humans.
The parts of the ear have mass and stiffness, so they cannot follow very rapid vibrations, and very slow vibrations do not make the cochlea produce signals.
The upper limit falls with age (older people often cannot hear above about 15 kHz) and after damage from loud noise.
Other animals have different ranges: dogs and bats hear ultrasound; elephants and whales detect infrasound.
Microphones and loudspeakers also only work over a limited range for the same reason: their moving parts can only vibrate effectively at certain frequencies.

callouts.p: Sound waves with a frequency **higher than 20 kHz**, above the upper limit of human hearing.

core.p: When a wave reaches a boundary between two different media, **some is reflected and some is transmitted**. Ultrasound is useful because each boundary inside an object sends back a small echo, while the rest of the wave carries on to the next boundary.
bullets: A **transducer** (probe) sends out short pulses of ultrasound and detects the reflected pulses (echoes).
Each echo comes from a boundary where the material changes, for example between soft tissue and bone, or metal and an air crack.
The **time** taken for each echo to return tells you how far away the boundary is.
The **strength** of the echo depends on how different the two materials are.
A computer combines echoes from many directions to build an image.
Ultrasound's short wavelength means it can show fine detail.

callouts.p: distance = speed x time, and for an echo the wave travels there and back, so **depth = (speed x time) / 2**.

core.p: Because it is partially reflected at boundaries and is non-ionising, ultrasound is used to see inside things without cutting them open.
bullets: **Medical imaging**: pre-natal scans of a fetus, and scans of organs; it is safe because it is **not ionising**, unlike X-rays.
**Industrial imaging (flaw detection)**: finding cracks or defects inside metal castings, welds or rail tracks. A crack gives an extra echo that returns sooner than the echo from the far side.
**Echo sounding / SONAR**: measuring the depth of water and locating shoals of fish, wrecks or submarines.
Ultrasound is also used in cleaning delicate objects, but that is not an imaging use.

callouts.t: Why not X-rays for a fetus?
callouts.p: X-rays are **ionising** and could damage the fetus's cells and DNA; ultrasound is non-ionising, so it is safer.

core.p: **SONAR** (sound navigation and ranging) is the use of ultrasound pulses in water to detect objects and measure distances.
bullets: A ship's transducer sends a pulse of ultrasound down into the water.
The pulse reflects from the sea bed (or a shoal of fish, or a wreck) and the echo returns to the ship.
The time between sending the pulse and receiving the echo is measured.
Using the speed of sound in water (about 1500 m/s): depth = (speed x time) / 2.
Bats and dolphins use a natural version called **echolocation**.

core.p: Earthquakes produce **seismic waves** that travel through the Earth. They are detected by **seismometers** at stations around the world.
bullets: **P waves** (primary) are **longitudinal**: rock vibrates parallel to the direction of travel.
P waves are faster and arrive first; they can travel through **solids and liquids**.
**S waves** (secondary) are **transverse**: rock vibrates at right angles to the direction of travel.
S waves are slower and arrive later; they can travel through **solids only**, not liquids.
Liquids cannot transmit S waves because liquid particles can slide past each other and do not pull their neighbours sideways.
Both types change speed as the density and type of rock change, so their paths **curve** (refraction) and they refract sharply at boundaries between layers.

core.h: Seismic evidence for the Earth's structure
core.p: No one can drill to the centre of the Earth, so scientists use seismic waves to detect its hidden structure. The pattern of where P and S waves are and are not detected is the key evidence.
bullets: The Earth has a **crust**, a solid **mantle**, a **liquid outer core** and a **solid inner core**.
S waves are **not detected** on a large part of the far side of the Earth from an earthquake: the **S-wave shadow zone** (beyond about 105 degrees from the epicentre).
Because S waves cannot pass through liquids, this shadow shows that the **outer core is liquid**.
P waves are detected on the far side but there is a **P-wave shadow zone** (roughly 105 to 140 degrees) where few are received, because P waves **refract** at the mantle/core boundary.
The size of the shadow zones lets scientists calculate the **size of the core**.
Faint P waves in the P shadow zone, refracted by the inner core, gave evidence for a solid inner core.
The curved paths show that wave speed changes gradually with depth (density increases).

callouts.p: **S waves do not travel through liquids** + **S waves are not detected on the far side** => **the outer core is liquid**.

core.h: Using seismic data to locate an earthquake
core.p: Because P waves travel faster than S waves, the gap between their arrival times at a seismometer depends on how far away the earthquake was.
bullets: The further away the earthquake, the longer the time gap between the P wave and S wave arriving.
Using the time gap at three or more stations, scientists can work out the distance from each and locate the epicentre.
This uses the same idea as echo timing: distance = speed x time.

core.h: Calculations with echoes and seismic waves
core.p: The equation distance = speed x time is used throughout this topic. The main trap is remembering whether the time is for one way or there and back.
bullets: **distance travelled = speed x time** (metres, metres per second, seconds).
For an echo, the measured time is for the round trip, so **one-way distance = speed x time / 2**.
Rearranged: time = distance / speed; speed = distance / time.
Convert units: milliseconds (ms) to seconds by dividing by 1000; microseconds by dividing by 1 000 000; km to m by multiplying by 1000.
wave speed = frequency x wavelength can be used to find the wavelength of ultrasound in a medium.

callouts.p: Forgetting to divide by 2 for an echo is the most common way to lose a mark.

core.p: All of these uses rely on the same physics: a wave is sent into something we cannot see inside, and the way it is **reflected, refracted, transmitted or absorbed** at hidden boundaries is measured.
bullets: Ultrasound and SONAR: measure **reflection** times at boundaries.
Seismic waves: measure which waves are **transmitted** and where they are **refracted**.
Comparing what arrives with what was sent tells us about the materials and boundaries inside.
Different waves are chosen to suit the job: ultrasound for small, fine detail; low-frequency seismic waves for the whole Earth.

analogy.p: Clap in a canyon and time the echo: the longer the wait, the further the cliff, and the sound has gone there and back so you halve the distance. Ultrasound scanners and SONAR do exactly this, but with millions of very short, high-pitched claps, and they listen for echoes from every hidden boundary, not just one cliff. For seismic waves, imagine shouting into a building with a swimming pool in the middle: a shove that relies on sideways grip (S wave) cannot cross the water, so people behind the pool feel nothing, revealing the pool is there. Where it breaks down: real echoes are only partial (most of the wave carries on), and seismic waves curve gradually as rock density changes rather than travelling in straight lines.

terms.d: A wave in which the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, for example sound and P waves.
A wave in which the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer, for example S waves.
A thin membrane in the ear that vibrates when sound waves in air reach it.
The fluid-filled part of the inner ear where vibrations are converted into electrical signals.
About 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear.
Sound with a frequency above 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear.
A reflected sound or ultrasound wave.
A device that produces ultrasound pulses and detects the returning echoes.
When part of a wave is reflected at a boundary between two media and the rest is transmitted.
Using pulses of sound or ultrasound in water and timing their echoes to find the distance to objects or the sea bed.
Waves produced by earthquakes that travel through the Earth.
A longitudinal seismic wave that travels through solids and liquids and arrives first.
A transverse seismic wave that travels through solids only and is slower than a P wave.
A region of the Earth's surface where a type of seismic wave from an earthquake is not detected.
An instrument that detects and records seismic waves.

mistakes.w: Ultrasound is a type of electromagnetic wave.
mistakes.r: Ultrasound is a **sound** wave (longitudinal, mechanical) with frequency above 20 kHz.

mistakes.w: Depth = speed x time (no halving) for an echo.
mistakes.r: The echo time is for the journey **there and back**, so depth = speed x time / 2.

mistakes.w: S waves cannot travel through the core.
mistakes.r: S waves cannot travel through **liquids**, so they cannot pass through the **liquid outer core**.

mistakes.w: P waves are transverse and S waves are longitudinal.
mistakes.r: **P waves are longitudinal**, **S waves are transverse**.

mistakes.w: Sound travels fastest in air.
mistakes.r: Sound is generally **fastest in solids** because particles are close and strongly bonded.

mistakes.w: The frequency of sound changes when it enters a solid.
mistakes.r: The **frequency stays the same**; the speed and wavelength change.

mistakes.w: Ultrasound is used for pre-natal scans because it is cheaper.
mistakes.r: It is used because it is **non-ionising**, so it does not damage cells, unlike X-rays.

mistakes.w: All of the ultrasound is reflected at the first boundary.
mistakes.r: Ultrasound is **partially** reflected: some is reflected and the rest is transmitted to deeper boundaries.

mistakes.w: We can hear any frequency if it is loud enough.
mistakes.r: The ear only works over a **limited frequency range** (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz) because of how its parts vibrate.

exam.q: State the approximate range of frequencies that humans can hear.
model: 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)
exam.tip: Include units.

exam.q: What is ultrasound?
model: Sound with a frequency above 20 kHz (above the range of human hearing)
exam.tip: Say 'sound', not just 'high frequency wave'.

exam.q: Describe how sound waves in air cause us to hear.
model: Sound waves (pressure variations) travel into the ear canal
They make the eardrum vibrate
Vibrations pass through the small bones to the cochlea
Cochlea produces electrical signals sent along the nerve to the brain
exam.tip: Follow the order: air, eardrum, bones, cochlea, nerve, brain.

exam.q: Suggest why humans cannot hear sounds above 20 kHz.
model: Conversion of sound into vibrations of the eardrum/bones only works over a limited frequency range
Parts of the ear cannot vibrate fast enough / respond at such high frequencies
exam.tip: Link to the solid parts of the ear.

exam.q: A ship sends an ultrasound pulse down to the sea bed. The echo returns after 0.40 s. The speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea.
model: distance = speed x time = 1500 x 0.40 = 600 m
This is there and back, so divide by 2
depth = 300 m
exam.tip: Halve for an echo.

exam.q: Explain why ultrasound rather than X-rays is used to scan a fetus.
model: X-rays are ionising and can damage cells/DNA of the fetus
Ultrasound is non-ionising so is safer
exam.tip: Use the word ionising.

exam.q: Describe two differences between P waves and S waves.
model: P waves are longitudinal, S waves are transverse
P waves travel through solids and liquids, S waves through solids only (or P waves are faster)
exam.tip: Give both sides of each comparison.

exam.q: Explain how ultrasound can be used to find a crack inside a metal block.
model: Ultrasound pulse sent into the metal by a transducer
Pulse partially reflected at the boundary with the crack
Echo from the crack returns before the echo from the far side of the block
Time of echo used with speed to calculate depth of crack (depth = speed x time / 2)
exam.tip: Mention the extra, earlier echo.

exam.q: Explain how seismic waves provide evidence for the structure of the Earth.
model: Earthquakes produce P (longitudinal) and S (transverse) waves detected by seismometers around the world
S waves cannot travel through liquids
S waves are not detected in a large shadow zone on the opposite side of the Earth
So the outer core must be liquid
P waves refract at the boundary between mantle and core, producing a P-wave shadow zone
The paths curve because wave speed changes with depth; size of shadow zones gives the size of the core
exam.tip: Level 3 needs the link from observation (shadow zone) to conclusion (liquid outer core) explained, not just stated.

exam.q: Sound travels from air into a steel rail. State what happens to its speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: Speed increases
Frequency stays the same
Wavelength increases
exam.tip: Use v = f x wavelength with f fixed.

exam.q: An ultrasound pulse takes 50 microseconds to return from a boundary inside the body. The speed of ultrasound in tissue is 1540 m/s. Calculate the depth of the boundary.
exam.tip: Convert microseconds first.

worked.q: A fishing boat's SONAR detects two echoes: one after 0.020 s from a shoal of fish and one after 0.080 s from the sea bed. Speed of sound in water = 1500 m/s. Find the depth of the fish and of the sea bed.
steps: Fish: distance there and back = 1500 x 0.020 = 30 m.
Fish depth = 30 / 2 = 15 m.
Sea bed: distance there and back = 1500 x 0.080 = 120 m.
Sea bed depth = 120 / 2 = 60 m.
worked.ans: Fish at 15 m depth, sea bed at 60 m depth.

worked.q: Ultrasound of frequency 2.0 MHz travels through tissue at 1540 m/s. Calculate its wavelength.
steps: wave speed = frequency x wavelength, so wavelength = speed / frequency.
frequency = 2.0 MHz = 2.0 x 10^6 Hz.
worked.ans: 7.7 x 10^-4 m (0.77 mm), short enough to show fine detail.

worked.q: A seismometer on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake records P waves but no S waves. Explain what this tells scientists.
steps: S waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids.
To reach the opposite side, waves must pass through the core.
P waves (longitudinal) can pass through liquids, so they arrive.
S waves do not arrive, so part of the core must be liquid.
worked.ans: It is evidence that the Earth's outer core is liquid.
